Earth's surface is always changing. Some changes are slow. Other changes are very fast.

Slow Changes

Wind and rain break rock into tiny pieces. This is called weathering. Water and wind carry the pieces away. This is called erosion. Later, the pieces drop in a new place. This is called deposition. A river can alter a valley this way, but it takes thousands of years.

Fast Changes

Some changes happen in minutes. A volcano can erupt and cover the land with hot lava. After heavy rain, a hillside can collapse in a landslide. These fast events can cause great destruction to homes and roads.

Staying Safe

A volcano or a steep hill can be a hazard. Scientists watch these places closely. They check the ground for small shakes and cracks. Towns make plans so people know where to go. When a severe storm comes, families follow the plan. Good planning can stop a crisis before it starts.

Slow or fast, Earth keeps changing. People can learn to live safely with these changes.

ON.body:
The ground under your feet may seem solid and still, but Earth's surface is always changing. Some changes are so slow that no one notices them. Others happen so quickly that they make the evening news.

Slow and Steady

Over many years, rain, ice, and wind break rocks into smaller pieces. Scientists call this weathering. Moving water and wind then carry the pieces away, a process called erosion. When the water slows down, it drops the sand and soil somewhere new. This is deposition. Together, these three processes can alter a whole landscape. A tiny stream can carve a deep canyon, but only after thousands of years.

Sudden and Strong

Fast changes are different. A volcano can erupt with little warning, sending ash and lava across nearby land. After days of heavy rain, the soil on a steep hill can become so heavy that the slope collapses. Within minutes, a landslide can cause substantial destruction to houses, farms, and roads.

Getting Ready

Because nature can be unpredictable, communities work hard to reduce the danger. Scientists place instruments on volcanoes to measure tiny earthquakes and rising gas. Engineers build walls and plant trees to hold soil in place on hillsides. Towns write emergency plans that tell families where to go if a severe event happens. When people know a hazard is coming, a possible crisis can become a problem they can manage.

Both slow and fast changes shape the land we live on. Understanding them helps people stay safe.

ABOVE.body:
Mountains look permanent, and a river valley seems as if it has always been there. In reality, Earth's surface is constantly being reshaped. Some of these changes are gradual and almost invisible, while others arrive suddenly and leave a landscape unrecognizable within hours.

The Gradual Forces

Three slow processes work together like a team. First, weathering breaks rock apart as rain seeps into cracks, water freezes and expands, and plant roots push stone aside. Next, erosion transports the loosened fragments, carried along by rivers, glaciers, and wind. Finally, deposition occurs when the moving water or air loses energy and drops its load, building beaches, sandbars, and wide river deltas. Over thousands of years, this partnership can alter an entire region, grinding mountains down and filling valleys up.

The Sudden Forces

In contrast, some events transform the land almost instantly. When pressure builds beneath a volcano, an eruption can bury fields under ash and lava. On steep slopes soaked by heavy rain, the soil can lose its grip and collapse in a landslide. These rapid events can cause substantial destruction, and because they are unpredictable, they are especially dangerous to nearby communities.

Reducing the Risk

People cannot stop natural hazards, but they can prepare for them. Scientists monitor volcanoes with sensors that detect small earthquakes and changes in gas. Engineers reinforce hillsides with retaining walls, drainage pipes, and deep-rooted plants. Local governments design evacuation routes and practice emergency drills, so residents know exactly what to do when a severe warning is announced. Careful preparation can prevent a dangerous event from becoming a full crisis.

Whether the change takes a million years or a single afternoon, the lesson is the same: Earth is never finished changing, and understanding how it changes is the first step toward living safely upon it.

Maya and Leen were best friends. When the school talent show was announced, Leen said, “We'll sing together!” Maya did not answer. She wanted to do a magic act by herself.

All week, Leen made plans for both of them. She picked the song. She picked matching shirts. Maya hesitated each time she tried to speak. She felt uncomfortably quiet inside.

At home, Maya told her grandmother. “I desperately want to do my own act,” she said. “But I don't want to hurt Leen.”

Grandmother smiled. “I will advise you the way my mother advised me,” she said. “Speak from your heart. A true friend will listen. You are accountable for your own choices.”

The next day, Maya told Leen the truth. Leen looked surprised. Then she nodded. “I should have asked you,” she said.

On the night of the show, Leen sang and Maya did her magic tricks. Each girl cheered for the other. Maya felt proud. Her grandmother had been her inspiration.

questions.why: Maya was nervous and unsure, so she stopped before speaking. That is what hesitated means.

ON.body:
When Ms. Haddad announced the school talent show, Leen grabbed Maya's arm. “We'll sing a duet, like always!” she said. Maya smiled, but her stomach twisted. For months she had practiced card tricks in her room, and she dreamed of performing a magic act on her own.

All week Leen made decisions for both of them. She chose the song, the matching yellow shirts, and even the way they would bow. Every time Maya opened her mouth to explain, she hesitated. The words seemed stuck, and she sat uncomfortably while Leen talked on and on.

That evening, Maya sat with her grandmother on the balcony. “I desperately want to do magic,” she admitted, “but if I tell Leen, she might feel humiliated in front of everyone.”

Her grandmother set down her tea. “Let me advise you,” she said gently. “Keeping quiet is not the same as being kind. Your self-esteem grows when you speak honestly. You are accountable for your own voice, and a real friend wants to hear it.”

The next morning, Maya found Leen by the lockers. Her heart was pounding, but she said, “Leen, I love singing with you, but this time I want to do a magic act alone.”

Leen was quiet for a moment. Then she sighed. “I never asked what you wanted,” she said. “I'm sorry.”

On the night of the show, Leen sang a solo, and Maya pulled a scarf from an empty hat. The girls cheered loudest for each other. Later, Maya told her grandmother that she had been her inspiration.

ABOVE.body:
The poster went up on a Monday: Annual Talent Show, Auditions Friday. Before Maya had finished reading it, Leen had already decided. “Our duet is going to be legendary,” she announced, linking arms with Maya as if the matter were settled.

Maya forced a smile. What Leen did not know was that every night for three months, Maya had practiced sleight-of-hand tricks in front of her bedroom mirror. She could make a coin vanish and a folded card reappear inside a sealed envelope. More than anything, she wanted to stand alone on that stage and hear the gasp of a surprised audience.

As the week went on, Leen took charge of everything: the song, the matching yellow shirts, the dramatic bow at the end. Each time Maya gathered her courage, she hesitated, and the moment slipped away. She sat uncomfortably through every rehearsal, feeling smaller and smaller.

On Wednesday evening she confessed everything to her grandmother. “I desperately want to perform my own act,” she said, “but if I back out now, Leen will be humiliated.”

Her grandmother listened without interrupting. Then she said, “I won't tell you what to do, but I will advise you to remember this: silence that hides your true feelings slowly damages a friendship. Your self-esteem depends on being honest with yourself first. You are accountable for your own choices, and so is Leen.”

The next morning, Maya waited by the lockers, rehearsing the sentence in her head. When Leen arrived, the words tumbled out. To Maya's astonishment, Leen did not storm away. Instead, she looked down at her shoes. “I've been bossy, haven't I?” she admitted. “I should have asked.”

On the night of the show, Leen sang a solo that made the audience clap along, and Maya made a silk scarf bloom from an empty hat. Afterward, the friends hugged backstage. Maya realized that honesty had not broken their friendship; it had made it stronger. Her grandmother, she decided, was her greatest inspiration.

Can a business make money and help people at the same time? Many people say yes.

A business is an enterprise that sells things people want. It needs to earn money to pay its workers. But some business owners are also compassionate. They care about people who need help.

One Pair for Another

Some shoe companies use a special process. For every pair of shoes they sell, they give a pair to a child who has none. Customers like this idea. They feel good when they buy the shoes.

Raising Funds

Other businesses raise funds for good causes. A bakery might give part of its money from one day each month to a hospital. A shop might collect coins at the counter for a school in need. Over time, these small gifts add up.

A Smart Plan

Helping others can become part of a company's routine. It is an innovative way to do business. People trust a company that cares. That trust brings more customers.

Businesses can do well and do good. Both goals can work together.

ON.body:
Businesses exist to make money. Yet many people believe a company can earn a profit and improve the world at the same time. Evidence from successful companies suggests they are right.

Giving with Every Sale

Some companies have built kindness directly into the way they sell. A shoe company, for example, might follow a simple process: every time a customer buys a pair, the company donates a pair to a child who needs one. This innovative plan turns an ordinary purchase into a gift. Customers often choose these products because they want their money to make a difference.

Supporting the Community

Other businesses raise funds for charities and community projects. A local restaurant may donate a share of one night's earnings to a children's hospital. A grocery store may invite shoppers to round up their bill and give the extra coins to a food bank. Each gift seems small, but together these donations can pay for meals, books, or medical care.

Why It Works

When helping becomes part of a company's routine, everyone can benefit. Workers feel proud of where they work. Customers return because they trust a compassionate brand. In many cases, an undertaking that began as a kind gesture actually helps the enterprise grow.

An exceptional business is not measured only by how much money it makes. It can also be measured by how many lives it improves. The most successful companies show that profit and kindness do not have to compete; they can work as partners.

ABOVE.body:
For a long time, many people assumed that a business had only one purpose: to make as much money as possible. Charity, they believed, was a separate activity for volunteers and governments. Today, a growing number of companies are proving that this division is unnecessary. A well-run enterprise can be financially successful while also meeting real needs in the community.

Kindness Built into the Product

One approach is to make giving part of the product itself. A shoe company, for instance, can promise that for every pair sold, another pair will be delivered to a child who walks barefoot. Because the donation happens automatically, it becomes part of the company's daily routine rather than an occasional event. This innovative model also gives customers a powerful reason to buy: their purchase becomes an act of generosity.

Partnerships That Raise Funds

Another approach is to raise funds for organizations that already help people. Restaurants hold special evenings when a portion of the earnings goes to a children's hospital. Supermarkets invite shoppers to round up their bills, collecting spare change for local food banks. Although each contribution is modest, thousands of small gifts can finance meals, school supplies, and medical equipment.

The Business Case for Caring

Critics sometimes argue that donations reduce profits. However, compassionate companies often discover the opposite. Employees are more motivated when they believe their work matters, and customers remain loyal to brands they trust. In this way, a charitable undertaking can strengthen the very company that funds it, creating a cycle in which success and service support each other.

An exceptional business, therefore, should not be judged only by its earnings report. It should also be judged by the difference it makes. The examples above demonstrate that profit and purpose are not rivals; when they are combined thoughtfully, both can grow.

Animals live in many kinds of places. Some places are cold. Some are hot. Animals have special body parts and actions that help them live there. These are called adaptations.

Staying Hidden

Some animals are camouflaged. Their color matches the place where they live. A white hare is hard to see in the snow. This helps it hide from a predator, an animal that hunts it.

Catching Food

Other adaptations help animals catch prey. A cat has soft paws, so it can walk quietly. Then it can pounce on a mouse. Some snakes are poisonous. One bite can stop their prey from running away.

Using Special Senses

Some animals feel vibrations in the ground. An elephant can sense a far-away herd through its feet. A spider feels its web shake when an insect lands in it.

Staying Warm

A polar bear has thick fur and a layer of fat. These keep it warm in icy water.

Adaptations are extraordinary. They help animals hide, hunt, and stay alive.

ON.body:
Every environment on Earth has its own challenges. Deserts are dry, oceans are deep, and the Arctic is freezing. To survive, animals have developed adaptations, special body features and behaviors that help them live where they do.

Hiding in Plain Sight

Many animals are camouflaged. Their colors or patterns blend into their surroundings. An arctic fox wears a white coat in winter, then turns brown in summer to match the rocks. Because it is hard to spot, a predator may walk right past it.

Tools for Hunting

Predators have adaptations for catching prey. A tiger's striped fur lets it creep through tall grass before it pounces. Some snakes are poisonous; their venom quickly weakens an animal so it cannot escape. An archerfish even dribbles a stream of water from its mouth to knock insects off leaves.

Super Senses

Some adaptations work like built-in alarms. Elephants can detect vibrations in the ground made by other elephants many kilometers away. A spider sits still until it feels its web tremble, and then it rushes out to grab its meal.

Built for the Cold

In the Arctic, polar bears have thick fur and a layer of fat called blubber. Even their black skin helps them soak up heat from the sun.

From color to senses to fur, these extraordinary features allow animals to protect themselves, find food, and survive in difficult places. Each adaptation is a clue to how an animal lives.

ABOVE.body:
Imagine trying to survive in a place where the temperature drops far below freezing, or where food is scarce and enemies are everywhere. Animals face these challenges every day. Over many generations, species have developed adaptations, inherited physical features and behaviors that make survival in a particular environment possible.

The Art of Disappearing

One of the most effective adaptations is camouflage. A camouflaged animal blends so completely into its background that it becomes nearly invisible. The arctic fox grows a thick white coat for the snowy winter and then sheds it for a brown-gray coat that matches summer rocks. A leaf-tailed gecko, flattened against tree bark, can be impossible to see even from a short distance. Such disguises protect prey from hungry predators.

Weapons and Tricks

Predators, in turn, possess adaptations for capturing a meal. A tiger's stripes break up the outline of its body in tall grass, allowing it to approach silently before it pounces. Certain snakes are poisonous, delivering venom that quickly overpowers an animal. Perhaps most surprising is the archerfish, which dribbles a precise jet of water from its mouth to knock insects off overhanging leaves.

Sensing the Invisible

Other animals rely on senses far sharper than our own. Elephants detect low vibrations traveling through the ground, allowing them to communicate with distant herds. Spiders interpret the faintest trembling of their webs, distinguishing a trapped insect from a falling leaf.

Surviving the Extremes

In polar regions, the polar bear depends on dense fur and a thick layer of blubber, while its black skin absorbs warmth from sunlight. Even the soles of its enormous paws are covered with fur, which grips the ice and prevents slipping.

These extraordinary adaptations reveal a remarkable truth: every feature of an animal, from the color of its coat to the sensitivity of its feet, tells a story about the environment that shaped it.

CHARACTERS: ANT, GRASSHOPPER, BEETLE

SETTING: A green field in the rainy season.

(ANT carries a seed. GRASSHOPPER lies on a leaf.)

GRASSHOPPER: Ant, why are you working? Come and rest!

ANT: The dry season is coming. I must save food.

GRASSHOPPER: (laughing) You have a cranky attitude. Relax!

ANT: Saving food is my specialty. I like to be ready.

NARRATOR: Many weeks pass. Now the field is dry and brown.

(GRASSHOPPER walks slowly. He is hungry.)

Dog

My dog runs fast across the yard,
his tail a flag that waves.
He digs a hole, he finds a bone,
he guards it like he saves.

His nose is like a little drum
that taps against my hand.
He is a rocket on the grass,
a tiger in the sand.

At night he curls up by my bed,
his outstretched paws so still.
I love my dog, my furry friend,
I always will, I will.

Three Small Poems (Haiku)

Eagle
Wings wide in the sky,
the eagle rides on the wind,
a king of the clouds.

Chimp
Chimp swings branch to branch,
pokes a stick into the ground,
snack time, clever friend!

Winter Leaf
Brittle leaf falls down,
crunching under my small boots,
winter says hello.

About These Poems

Poets use descriptive words to help us see things. A simile compares two things using like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another thing. Rhyme is when words end with the same sound, like hand and sand.

Dog

He waits for me beside the gate,
a furry clock that's never late;
the moment that he hears my shoe
he spins as if he's brand new.

His tail's a flag of happy gold,
his eyes are warm when days are cold;
he races leaves across the lawn,
a comet till the light is gone.

And when I'm sad, he seems to know:
he rests his chin against my toe,
his outstretched paws, his patient sigh,
as steady as the evening sky.

Three Haiku of Wild Things

Eagle
Wide wings slice the wind,
eyes as sharp as winter ice,
the sky is her road.

Chimpanzee
A twig for a spoon,
he fishes termites from mud,
a creative chef.

Autumn Path
Brittle leaves whisper
beneath the fox's soft feet,
the woods hold their breath.

A Note on the Poems

The first poem is a lyric poem. It shares the speaker's feelings and uses rhyme and a steady beat, called meter. The haiku follow a pattern of three short lines. Both kinds of poems use descriptive language, including similes and metaphors, so readers can picture each animal in a fresh way. As you read, notice how each poet feels about the animal. Dog

At dusk he stations by the gate,
a furry sentry, never late;
he reads the street with eager nose
and knows my footstep from all those.

His tail becomes a beating drum,
his whole self shouts that I have come;
he chases sparrows, never quite,
a comet streaking through the light.

But when the day has bruised my heart,
he seems to sense it from the start:
he lays his chin upon my knee,
his outstretched paws an anchor to me.

He asks for nothing: just a walk,
a scratch, a bit of gentle talk;
and in return, through sun and storm,
he is a hearth that keeps me warm.

Three Haiku of the Wild

Eagle
Wings like silver sails
unfold above the canyon,
the wind is her throne.

Chimpanzee
He strips a green stem,
angles it into the mound,
an inventor's feast.

First Frost
Brittle grasses snap
beneath a deer's careful hooves,
the meadow shivers.

Thinking About the Poems

“Dog” is a lyric poem, a poem that expresses the speaker's personal emotions. It uses rhyming pairs of lines and a regular meter, which give it a gentle, song-like rhythm. The haiku, in contrast, are brief and unrhymed, capturing a single image in three lines. Both forms rely on descriptive, figurative language. Similes compare using like or as, while metaphors make bolder claims, declaring that one thing simply is another. These creative choices invite readers to see ordinary animals in extraordinary ways.

Notice, too, how perspective shapes each poem. The speaker of “Dog” describes a personal companion, so the language is tender and grateful. The haiku poets observe wild animals from a distance, and their words express admiration rather than affection: the eagle is royal, the chimpanzee is inventive, and even the meadow seems alive. The same tools of language can create very different feelings depending on who is speaking and why.

When Mr. Ortiz assigned our class a community service project, everyone started shouting ideas. I stayed quiet, because one word on the board, storm, had carried me back in time.

I was seven when Hurricane Katrina struck New Orleans. I remember the wind screaming against our windows all night and my mother holding a flashlight. In the morning, our street looked like a brown river. Our home stood on higher ground, so we were safe, but the houses near the canal were not. Residents waded through the water carrying whatever they could save. Furniture, photographs, and toys were scattered across lawns.

My best friend, Tasha, lived near the canal. Days later, I saw her standing in front of her ruined house, holding a muddy stuffed rabbit. She didn't cry. She just stared. I didn't know what to say, so I gave her my baseball cap. It was all I had.

Now I'm eleven, and I feel more mature. I knew exactly what I wanted to do. “Let's collect toys for kids who lose their homes in disasters,” I said.

My friends liked the idea. We placed boxes around the school and made posters. We had to be selective: only clean toys in good condition. When the boxes overflowed, we gingerly wrapped each toy in paper. Two relief organizations agreed to deliver them to families after the next big storm.

The generosity of my classmates amazed me. Some kids gave away toys they still loved. As I taped the last box shut, I thought about Tasha and that muddy rabbit. This time, I had more than a baseball cap to give.

On the whiteboard, under the heading Ways to Help, someone had written the word storm, and that single word pulled me back six years.

I was seven when Hurricane Katrina roared into New Orleans. I remember lying awake while the wind shrieked around the house and rain hammered the roof like fists. My mother sat beside me with a flashlight, humming to cover the noise. By morning, our street had become a slow brown river. Because our house sat on a slight rise, the water stopped at our porch steps. The neighborhood near the canal was not so fortunate. Residents waded through waist-deep water carrying children and pets, and the belongings they had left behind were scattered across lawns and sidewalks.

My best friend, Tasha, lived near that canal. A week later I found her standing silently in front of what remained of her house, clutching a stuffed rabbit caked with mud. I wanted to say something wise, but I was too young to find the words. Instead, I pulled off my baseball cap and placed it on her head. It seemed like such a small gesture.

Now, at thirteen, I am more mature, and I understood immediately what I wanted to do. “Let's collect toys for children who lose their homes in disasters,” I said.

The idea caught on. We decorated collection boxes and hung posters in every hallway. We were selective, accepting only clean toys in good condition, because we wanted each child to feel they had received a real gift. When the boxes overflowed, we gingerly wrapped each item in tissue paper. Two disaster-relief organizations agreed to deliver everything wherever families needed help next.

The generosity of my classmates astonished me. Some gave away favorite toys they had owned for years. As I sealed the final box, I pictured Tasha in my oversized cap, holding that muddy rabbit. Back then, a cap was all I could offer. This time, I could offer much more.

In the hollows of southern West Virginia, steep green mountains rise above narrow valleys. This is where Judy Bonds was born in 1952. Her father and grandfather worked in coal mines, and Judy grew up proud of her community, its fresh streams, and its close-knit families.

A Changing Landscape

By the 1990s, mining in her region had changed dramatically. Instead of digging tunnels, some companies used explosives to blast away the tops of mountains, a method called mountaintop removal. Forests were cut down, rocks and dirt were dumped into valleys, and coal dust drifted into homes. Many families felt mistreated, yet they worried that complaining might cost their neighbors' jobs.

A Turning Point

One afternoon Judy's young grandson stood in a creek holding a handful of dead fish and asked what was wrong with them. For Judy, that moment changed everything. She recognized an injustice that was harming the health of her own family.

Taking a Stand

Judy joined a local group working to protect the mountains and eventually became one of its leaders. She was not a lawyer or a scientist, but she believed living in the hollow made her qualified to speak. She organized peaceful protests, testified at hearings, and gave encouragement to neighbors who were afraid to speak up. She urged people to make sure they were registered to vote. Some supporters even called for a boycott of companies they felt were harming the land.

In 2003, Judy received a major international award for environmental leaders. She worked to fulfill her promise to protect the mountains until her death in 2011. The author's view is clear: Judy Bonds proved that ordinary people can stand up to powerful forces when they speak the truth.

Coal has shaped life in the mountains of southern West Virginia for generations. Julia “Judy” Bonds was born there in 1952, into a family of coal miners. She grew up in a narrow hollow where children waded in clear creeks and neighbors knew each other by name. For most of her life, Judy saw coal as the backbone of her community.

A Mountain Disappears

During the 1990s, however, a new mining method spread through the region. Rather than tunneling underground, some companies used powerful explosives to blast away the summits of mountains, exposing the coal seams beneath. This practice, known as mountaintop removal, flattened forests and buried streams under tons of rock. Residents complained of dust settling on their porches, cracked foundations, and polluted water. Many felt mistreated, yet they hesitated to object because so many families depended on mining paychecks.

A Grandson's Question

The moment that transformed Judy's life was a simple one. Her grandson, standing in a creek near their home, lifted a handful of dead fish and asked her what had happened to them. Judy later explained that she could no longer ignore what was happening. To her, the destruction was an injustice that the people of the hollows should not have to accept.

A Voice for the Hollows

Judy joined a grassroots organization dedicated to protecting the mountains and eventually became its director. Although she had no formal training in science or law, she insisted that her lifetime in the hollows made her qualified to speak about them. She led peaceful protests, testified before officials, and offered encouragement to neighbors who feared speaking out. She urged supporters to make certain they were registered to vote, and some activists called for a boycott of companies they considered responsible for the damage.

In 2003, Judy received a prestigious international prize honoring grassroots environmental leaders. She continued to fulfill her commitment until her death in 2011.

The author presents Judy not as a flawless hero but as an ordinary grandmother whose courage grew from love for her home. Her story suggests that the most powerful voices sometimes belong to the people who have the most to lose.

They saved seeds from the sweetest melons and the strongest wheat so the next generation of plants would inherit those helpful characteristics. Today, scientists can make changes much faster by altering a plant's genes directly in a laboratory. This process is called genetic modification, and the plants it produces are known as GM crops.

The Case For GM Crops

Supporters see GM crops as important advancements in agriculture. Some GM corn and cotton have built-in resistance to insects, so farmers spray fewer chemicals. Other crops have been changed to survive droughts or salty soil. Scientists have even developed a type of rice with extra vitamin A, which could help children in places where that vitamin is hard to get. Supporters argue that such crops could help feed a growing world population.

The Case Against GM Crops

Not everyone agrees. Critics have raised concerns about whether eating GM foods for many years could have effects no one has noticed yet. Others worry that modified plants could cross-breed with wild plants, or that insects might develop resistance over time, creating new problems. Some people simply disagreed with the idea that humans should change nature so quickly.

My Claim

GM crops are already prevalent; they grow on millions of hectares around the world. Because they offer real benefits but also raise reasonable questions, I believe the best approach is careful, independent testing and clear labels. That way, scientists can keep improving crops, and families can make informed choices about the food they eat.

Long before laboratories existed, farmers were already shaping the crops they grew. By saving seeds from the hardiest wheat and the juiciest fruit, they ensured that the next generation of plants would inherit those desirable characteristics. This slow process of selection took centuries. Modern genetic modification accomplishes something similar in a fraction of the time: scientists identify a useful gene, sometimes from an entirely different organism, and insert it directly into a plant's cells.

Arguments in Favor

Supporters describe GM crops as some of the most significant advancements in modern agriculture. Certain varieties of corn and cotton produce a protein that gives them resistance to specific insect pests, reducing the need for chemical sprays. Other crops have been engineered to tolerate drought, flooding, or salty soil, conditions that are expected to become more common. One well-known example, a rice enriched with vitamin A, was designed to address a deficiency that can harm children's eyesight. With the world's population still rising, supporters argue that such tools could be essential for food security.

Arguments Against

Critics, however, have raised several concerns. Some question whether eating modified foods over many decades could have health effects that short studies cannot detect. Others point out that pests may eventually evolve resistance to engineered traits, just as bacteria adapt to medicines. There is also the possibility that modified genes could spread to wild relatives, with unpredictable consequences for ecosystems. Many people have disagreed on moral grounds, arguing that humans should not interfere with nature so directly.

Weighing the Evidence

GM crops are now prevalent across much of the world, so the question is no longer whether they will exist but how they should be managed. My claim is that the benefits are too important to ignore, but the risks are too real to dismiss. Independent long-term research, careful monitoring of the environment, and honest labeling would allow societies to gain the advantages of this technology while respecting people's right to know what they eat. A thoughtful middle path serves both science and the public better than either blind enthusiasm or automatic rejection.

Why We Have Laws

Laws keep people safe. A government makes laws and runs services like schools and fire stations. In a democracy, people vote for leaders. Those leaders write legislation, which is a group of new laws.

Working Together

When Rules Disappear

Without traffic laws, drivers would speed through intersections, and accidents would increase. Without trash collection, garbage would pile up on sidewalks, attracting rats and spreading disease. Factories might dump waste into rivers because no law would stop them, so the water people drink would become polluted. Playgrounds would fall apart, since no one would be responsible for repairing them. Eventually, people would feel unsafe in their own neighborhoods.

How Government Helps

That is why communities create governments. A government makes laws and provides public services such as police, firefighters, roads, and schools. In a democracy, citizens elect representatives who write and vote on legislation. Because people have different needs, lawmakers often must compromise, with each side accepting part of what it wants.

Rules That Can Change

Laws are not frozen forever. In the United States, the Constitution has been changed through amendments. One amendment gave women the right to vote; another lowered the voting age to eighteen. Each new version of the law reflects what citizens have learned over time.

Voting is both a right and a privilege. It requires a commitment to stay informed and take part. A world without rules might seem free, but the effects would quickly show that rules are what make freedom safe.

Imagine opening your eyes one morning to discover that every rule, law, and government office has disappeared. There are no speed limits, no garbage trucks, no courts, and no one to call in an emergency. For a few hours, this might feel like the ultimate freedom. Before long, however, a chain of consequences would begin.

A Chain Reaction

Without traffic laws, drivers would race through intersections, causing collisions and blocking roads. Ambulances, delayed by the chaos, would struggle to reach the injured. Without public sanitation, garbage would accumulate on every corner, attracting pests and spreading illness. Factories, freed from environmental regulations, could release chemicals into rivers, contaminating drinking water for entire cities. Public parks and libraries would deteriorate because no one would be assigned to maintain them. Eventually, fear would replace freedom, and people would retreat behind locked doors.

The Purpose of Government

This imagined world explains why human societies have always created some form of government. Governments establish laws that protect citizens' safety and rights, and they provide services that no single family could manage alone. In a democracy, power comes from the people: citizens elect representatives, and those representatives debate and pass legislation. Because citizens hold different opinions, the democratic process depends on compromise, in which opposing groups each accept part of what they want in order to reach an agreement.

A Living Framework

The laws of a democracy are designed to grow. The United States Constitution, for example, has been revised through amendments that expanded voting rights and protected individual freedoms. Each revised version reflects lessons the nation learned about fairness.

Participating in a democracy is a privilege, but it is also a responsibility. It demands a commitment to stay informed, to listen to people who disagree, and to vote. The thought experiment of a world without rules reveals a surprising truth: laws do not simply limit our freedom. In many ways, they are what make our freedom possible.

One morning, men came to town with tall poles and long wires. They were putting in telephones! My father, Dr. Reed, was excited. “This new technology will help me reach sick people faster,” he said.

Not everyone agreed. Mrs. Pell squirmed in her chair at the town meeting. “Why talk to a box?” she asked. “We can just walk to our neighbors.”

The engineers scouted the town for the best places to put the poles. Soon a gleaming black telephone hung on our kitchen wall. Father liked tinkering with it.

One night it rang. Mrs. Pell's grandson was very sick! Father grabbed his bag. Because of the phone, he got there in minutes. The boy got better.

In the spring of 1905, when I was eleven, the telephone came to Pine Hollow. Until then, news traveled by foot, by horse, or by the mail wagon that rattled into town twice a week.

The Town Divides

The engineering company sent two men who scouted every street, deciding where to plant the tall wooden poles. At the town meeting that night, opinions flew like sparks. My father, Dr. Reed, stood up. “This technology could save lives,” he said. “If someone falls ill at night, I could know in minutes instead of hours.”

Mrs. Pell, who ran the bakery, squirmed in her chair and crossed her arms. “A talking box on the wall? Next we'll stop visiting each other altogether. And who will be listening in?”

I could see both sides. I loved our quiet town, but I loved the idea of hearing a voice from miles away even more.

A Ring in the Night

By summer, a gleaming black telephone hung in our kitchen. Father spent evenings tinkering with it, while a young woman at the switchboard was busy directing calls across town. Many neighbors still refused to use one.

Then, one stormy night, our telephone jangled. It was the switchboard operator: Mrs. Pell's grandson had a high fever and was struggling to breathe. Father grabbed his bag and was out the door before the thunder faded. He reached the boy in time.

A Change of Heart

The next morning, Mrs. Pell appeared at our door holding a warm loaf of bread. “I was wrong about that talking box,” she said quietly.

Within a decade, nearly every home in Pine Hollow had its own telephone. I still remember that ring in the night as the moment our town decided to trust the future.

The Great Debate

The engineering company sent two men in dusty coats who scouted every street, measuring distances and marking trees with chalk. That evening, the town hall was so crowded that people stood along the walls. My father, Dr. Reed, rose to speak first. “This technology will change medicine in our town,” he declared. “When a child falls ill at midnight, I could be summoned in minutes rather than hours.”

Mrs. Pell, the baker, squirmed in her chair, her arms folded tightly. “I've heard the city folks praise these contraptions,” she replied. “But a voice in a box is not the same as a knock on the door. We'll stop visiting one another, and strangers at the switchboard will hear every word we say.”

Murmurs of agreement rippled through the room. I sat between my parents, torn. I treasured our slow, friendly town, yet the idea of speaking to someone miles away filled me with wonder.

The Night the Bell Rang

By summer, a gleaming black telephone was fastened to our kitchen wall. Father spent evenings tinkering with it, testing the crank and listening to the faint crackle while the operator was directing calls through her switchboard. Still, many families, including the Pells, refused to have one installed.

One stormy night in August, our telephone jangled so loudly that I sat straight up in bed. It was the operator. Mrs. Pell's grandson had a dangerous fever, and a neighbor with a telephone had called for help. Father seized his bag and vanished into the rain. He reached the boy in time.

A Loaf of Bread

The next morning, Mrs. Pell stood on our porch holding a warm loaf wrapped in cloth. “I judged that box too quickly,” she admitted. Within a decade, nearly every household in Pine Hollow had a telephone, and I have never forgotten the night when fear of the new gave way to gratitude.

Sing to Me

The piano keys looked big and cold,
my fingers small and slow.
I pressed a note, it sounded wrong,
I wanted just to go.

My teacher sat beside me there,
her hand was soft and kind.
“Sing to me the song,” she said,
“the one inside your mind.”

I tried again, I tried again,
I practiced every day,
until the music came to me
and I knew how to play.

The Tree

I looked up at the old oak tree,
its branches high and wide.
I slipped and fell, I slipped and fell,
but still I tried and tried.

My feet were dangling in the air,
a bird was hovering near.
I pulled up high, I reached the top,
and gave a happy cheer!

What a triumph! I did it!

the music, sweet and clear,
flew like a sparrow from my hands

The maple stood behind our school,
its lowest branch too high.

while clouds went drifting by.

my sneakers scraped and torn;
I found a knot to hold my foot

a dragonfly hovering near,
I pulled myself onto the branch;
the world looked new from here.

I whispered to the sky:
the top was never out of reach,
I only had to try.

and chased it with my hands,

and clouds rolled overhead.

to anchor my right shoe;

Some things are too small to see with just your eyes. To see them, scientists use a microscope. A microscope uses lenses to magnify things, or make them look bigger.

The First Microscopes

About 400 years ago, people in Europe made the first simple microscopes. They put two lenses in a tube. Things looked about ten times bigger.

A Closer Look

In the 1670s, a cloth seller named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made better lenses. He looked at a drop of pond water. He saw tiny living things swimming! No one had seen them before.

Modern Microscopes

In the 1930s, scientists built electron microscopes. These can make things look a million times bigger. Now scientists can see the tiny parts of cells.

What We Can See

Under a microscope, a typical snowflake shows six perfect arms. Sand looks gritty and full of tiny shells. Skin has tiny ridges and cells that cling together. On a humid day, you can even see tiny drops of water on a leaf.

Microscopes help us explore a world we cannot see.

ON.body:
Look closely at the back of your hand. You can see lines and maybe a few hairs. But there is a whole hidden world there that your eyes alone will never notice. To explore it, scientists rely on one of history's most important tools: the microscope.

The Earliest Lenses

Around 1590, spectacle makers in the Netherlands discovered that placing two curved lenses in a tube could magnify objects. These early instruments made things appear only about ten times larger, but they opened a door.

A Cloth Seller's Discovery

In the 1670s, a Dutch cloth merchant named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek began grinding his own tiny, powerful lenses. When he examined a drop of rainwater, he was astonished to see creatures he called animalcules wriggling and swimming. He had become the first person to observe bacteria and other single-celled life.

A Giant Leap

For centuries, microscopes used light. Then, in the 1930s, scientists invented the electron microscope, which uses beams of tiny particles instead. It can magnify objects more than a million times, revealing the inner parts of cells and even viruses.

The World Up Close

Today microscopes reveal remarkable detail. A typical snowflake reveals six delicate branches, each one unique. Beach sand, which feels gritty between your toes, turns out to contain broken shells and colorful crystals. Skin cells cling together like bricks in a wall, and salt crystals look like tiny cubes until water dissolves them. On a humid morning, droplets mingle on a leaf's surface like scattered jewels.

From simple tubes to powerful electron beams, microscopes have changed the way we understand life, health, and the natural world.

Every surface around you, from the skin on your fingertips to the dust on a windowsill, contains structures far too small for the human eye to detect. For most of history, this microscopic world was completely unknown. Its discovery depended on a single remarkable invention: the microscope.

The First Glimpse, Around 1590

Near the end of the sixteenth century, spectacle makers in the Netherlands found that two curved lenses mounted in a tube could magnify small objects. These compound microscopes were crude, enlarging objects only about ten times, and images were often blurry. Nevertheless, they hinted at a hidden level of nature waiting to be explored.

A Merchant Turned Scientist, the 1670s

The next breakthrough came from an unexpected source. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch cloth merchant, had used lenses to inspect the quality of fabric. Curious, he began grinding tiny, nearly perfect lenses of his own, achieving magnifications of more than two hundred times. When he examined a drop of rainwater, he described swarms of minute creatures darting in every direction. He had become the first person to observe bacteria and other single-celled organisms.

Beyond the Limits of Light, the 1930s

Optical microscopes eventually reached a limit, because light waves cannot reveal objects smaller than themselves. In the 1930s, scientists overcame this barrier with the electron microscope, which uses a focused beam of electrons. It can magnify specimens more than a million times, making the internal structures of cells and even individual viruses visible.

A Hidden Landscape

Modern microscopes reveal astonishing detail. A typical snowflake displays six intricate branches. Gritty beach sand contains fragments of shells and polished crystals. Skin cells cling together in overlapping layers, and salt crystals form tiny cubes until water dissolves them. On a humid morning, microscopic droplets mingle across a leaf's surface.

Each advance in microscope technology has allowed scientists to investigate diseases, develop medicines, and appreciate the complexity of the natural world.

On Saturday, Coach Lin took Sadie out of the game. Sadie had missed three shots. She sat on the bench. Her face felt hot, like a stove.

The gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn. Sadie spun her wheelchair toward the basket, caught the pass, and shot. The ball bounced off the rim. A minute later, she missed again, and then a third time.

Coach Lin waved her to the bench. “Take a breather, Sadie.”

Sadie's cheeks burned like hot coals. She had played wheelchair basketball for two years, ever since the accident that injured her spine. She was one of the fastest players on the team. Being pulled from a game felt like a door slammed in her face.

She glanced at the stands, searching for a familiar blue hoodie. It wasn't there. After her accident, her older brother Theo had pushed her through physical therapy and shouted encouragement at every game. This season, he had come to only one. He was always out with his friends now. Lately he felt like a stranger who just happened to live in her house.

At home, Sadie rolled straight to her room. A little later, Mom sat on the edge of the bed. “Rough game?”

The words poured out: the missed shots, the bench, the empty seat. “Theo doesn't care anymore,” Sadie said.

Mom was quiet for a moment. “Have you told him that you miss him?”

That evening, Sadie found Theo in the kitchen. Her heart pounded. “You used to come to all my games,” she said. “I miss you being there.”

Theo set down his sandwich. “I thought you didn't need me anymore,” he said slowly. “You're so good now.”

“I'll always need my biggest fan,” Sadie said.

The next Saturday, a blue hoodie sat in the front row. When Sadie sank her first basket, Theo's cheer filled the gym like a marching band.

The gym echoed with squeaking wheels and the steady thud of a dribbled ball. Sadie spun her chair around a defender, caught a bounce pass, and launched the shot she had practiced a thousand times. It clanged off the rim. Two possessions later she missed again, and then a third shot rolled lazily around the hoop before dropping out.

Coach Lin signaled from the sideline. “Sit this stretch out, Sadie. Reset.”

Sadie wheeled to the bench, her face burning like a furnace. Two years earlier, a car accident had injured her spine, and wheelchair basketball had become the place where she felt most like herself: quick, fearless, unstoppable. Being benched in front of everyone felt like being erased.

Out of habit, she scanned the bleachers for a faded blue hoodie. The seat in the front row was empty again. During the long months of rehabilitation, her older brother Theo had been her loudest cheerleader. He had pushed her chair up hospital ramps, invented silly games to make therapy bearable, and shouted her name at every tournament. This season, though, he had attended only one game. He spent his weekends with his friends, and when he was home, he was a closed door with headphones.

That evening Sadie retreated to her room. Her mother knocked softly and sat on the edge of the bed. “That was a tough game,” she said. Sadie had planned to say nothing, but the words broke loose like water through a dam: the missed shots, the bench, the empty seat.

“Have you told Theo any of this?” her mother asked gently.

Later, Sadie found Theo at the kitchen counter. Her pulse raced. “You used to come to every game,” she said. “I don't care if I score. I just miss seeing you there.”

Theo stared at his plate. “I figured you'd outgrown needing me,” he admitted. “You've gotten so strong. I thought I'd only be in the way.”

“You're never in the way,” Sadie said. “You're part of the reason I'm strong.”

The following Saturday, a faded blue hoodie occupied the front row. When Sadie's first shot swished through the net, Theo's cheer rolled across the gym like thunder.

In December 1606, three small ships, the Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery, sailed from England. On board were about 104 men and boys. Their expedition was paid for by a company that hoped to find gold and new trade routes in North America.

1607: A New Settlement

After a long, stormy voyage, the ships entered a wide river in Virginia in May 1607. The settlers chose a piece of land that was easy to defend and named it Jamestown, after King James I. Jamestown would become the first permanent English settlement in North America.

Tremendous Challenges

The location had serious problems. The river water near the fort was salty and unsafe to drink during the summer. Mosquitoes spread disease, and many settlers were more interested in searching for gold than in planting crops. Within months, more than half of them had died. The land already belonged to the Powhatan people, who sometimes traded corn with the newcomers and sometimes fought them to protect their homes.

1608: A Tough Leader

In 1608, Captain John Smith took charge. He announced a strict rule: those who did not work would not eat. He also traded with the Powhatan for food. His leadership helped the colony survive, at least for a while. After he left in 1609, a terrible winter called the Starving Time followed.

1994 to Today: Uncovering the Past

For many years, people thought the original fort had washed into the river. Then, in 1994, archaeologists began digging and found its walls. Since then, they have uncovered millions of objects. This archaeology provides evidence that helps historians compare what settlers wrote in each document with what really happened in that era.

In December 1606, three ships, the Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery, set sail from London carrying roughly 104 men and boys. Their expedition was financed by the Virginia Company, a group of investors who hoped the colonists would discover gold, valuable resources, and perhaps a water route to Asia.

Spring 1607: Choosing a Site

After more than four months at sea, the ships entered a broad river that the colonists named the James. In May 1607, they selected a narrow peninsula that seemed easy to defend from Spanish ships and established Jamestown, which became the first permanent English settlement in North America.

1607 to 1608: A Struggle to Survive

The site concealed tremendous dangers. During the summer, the river near the fort turned salty and polluted, and mosquitoes from the surrounding marshes spread disease. Many colonists, who were gentlemen unaccustomed to physical labor, spent their energy hunting for gold instead of planting crops. By winter, more than half had died. The surrounding land was home to the Powhatan, a powerful alliance of Native nations. Relations between the two groups shifted constantly between trade, especially for corn, and conflict over land.

1608 to 1610: Leadership and Hardship

When Captain John Smith became president of the colony in 1608, he imposed discipline with a blunt rule: anyone who refused to work would not eat. He also negotiated with the Powhatan for food. After Smith was injured and returned to England in 1609, the colony entered the Starving Time, a winter so severe that only a small fraction of the settlers survived.

1994 to the Present: Digging for Answers

For generations, historians assumed the original fort had eroded into the river. In 1994, however, archaeologists began excavating and uncovered the outline of its walls. Since then, the Jamestown Rediscovery project has recovered millions of artifacts, from armor and coins to the remains of meals. This archaeology supplies physical evidence that historians can compare with each written document from the era, revealing details the settlers never recorded, such as what they actually ate and how closely they interacted with the Powhatan.

“In two weeks,” Ms. Patel announced, “we'll hold the Great Energy Debate. Your job is to decide which energy source our town should use for the next fifty years.”

The class divided into teams, and each one began researching.

Team Fossil Fuels

Omar's team learned that coal, oil, and natural gas provide most of the world's electricity. They are reliable and produce power day and night. However, burning them releases gases that pollute the air and warm the planet. Another consequence is that these fuels took millions of years to form, so once they are used up, they are gone.

Team Sun and Wind

Lena's team discovered that solar and wind energy are renewable, which means nature keeps supplying them. By coincidence, a nearby library had just installed solar panels. The librarian showed the students how the panels converted sunlight into enough electricity to light the whole building. Wind turbines work in a similar way, using moving air. The challenge is that the sun sets and the wind sometimes stops, so batteries are needed to store extra power.

Team Biofuels

Jay's team studied biofuels, made from plants such as corn and sugarcane. They are renewable, but growing them requires huge fields, water, and fertilizer, land that could otherwise grow food.

Debate Day

The debate was lively. In the end, no single team won. The class realized that every source has advantages and disadvantages. Their final recommendation was to combine renewable sources, make homes more efficient, and consume less energy. “That,” said Ms. Patel, “is an incredible conclusion.”

“In two weeks,” Ms. Patel told her fourth graders, “our town council wants to hear your recommendations. Imagine you are planning how our community will get its energy for the next fifty years. Every claim you make must be supported by evidence.”

The room buzzed as students formed research teams.

The Case for Fossil Fuels

Omar's team investigated coal, oil, and natural gas, which still generate much of the world's electricity. Their greatest strength is reliability: power plants that burn them can operate at any hour, in any weather. Yet the team uncovered serious consequences. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and other pollutants that contribute to climate change and harm people's lungs. Moreover, these fuels formed over millions of years, so they cannot be replaced on any human timescale.

The Case for Sun and Wind

Lena's team focused on solar and wind power, both renewable resources that nature continually supplies. By coincidence, the public library had recently installed rooftop solar panels, and the librarian explained how the panels converted sunlight into electricity, supplying most of the building's needs on sunny days. Wind turbines, the team learned, turn the energy of moving air into electricity in a similar way. The drawback is that sunshine and wind are intermittent, so communities must invest in batteries or other storage to keep power flowing at night and on calm days.

The Case for Biofuels

Jay's team examined biofuels produced from crops such as corn and sugarcane. Although renewable, these fuels require vast amounts of farmland, water, and fertilizer, raising difficult questions about whether land should feed engines or people.

The Verdict

On debate day, each team defended its source with passion, but as the arguments unfolded, a pattern emerged: every option involved trade-offs. Rather than crowning a winner, the class presented a combined plan to the council. They recommended expanding solar and wind power, using natural gas only as a backup, making buildings more efficient, and encouraging residents to consume less. The council members were impressed. “What an incredible example of thinking critically,” one remarked. The students had learned that the best answers are often built from many good ideas.

It was the summer of 1805. Cameahwait was a chief of the Shoshone people. He lived in the mountains with his tribe.

Cameahwait often thought about his little sister. Years ago, enemy riders took her away. He had never stopped missing her.

One day, scouts brought news. Strangers were coming. They were explorers named Lewis and Clark. They needed horses to cross the tall mountains.

Some warriors did not trust the strangers. Cameahwait thought hard. He wanted to honor his ancestors by keeping his people safe. But he also knew that helping others was good.

The chief agreed to meet the explorers. A young woman was traveling with them. She would help them talk to the Shoshone.

When the woman saw Cameahwait, she jumped up. She ran to him and hugged him. She was crying! It was his lost sister, Sacagawea.

Cameahwait's heart was full. He gave the explorers the horses they needed. The long years apart were over.

Family, kindness, and working together had brought them joy.

In August of 1805, the mountain air was cool, and the rivers ran fast and clear. Cameahwait, a chief of the Lemhi Shoshone, stood at the edge of camp, watching the trail. Whenever the wind blew through the pines, he remembered his younger sister.

Years earlier, raiders from another nation had attacked the Shoshone hunting camp and carried several children away. His sister had been one of them. Cameahwait had searched for news of her, but the mountains had kept their silence.

Strangers on the Trail

Now scouts reported that pale-skinned strangers were approaching. Their leaders, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, were exploring a route to the Pacific Ocean. They urgently needed horses to cross the towering Bitterroot Mountains before winter.

Some warriors despised the idea of helping outsiders. “They may bring enemies,” one argued. Cameahwait felt the intensity of the debate. As chief, he had to honor his ancestors by protecting his people. Yet he also believed that trade and cooperation could make the Shoshone stronger.

The Meeting

Cameahwait chose to meet the explorers. Because no one spoke both languages, the group relied on a chain of translators. One of them was a young Shoshone woman traveling with the expedition, carrying her baby on her back.

As the talks began, the young woman suddenly stopped. She stared at Cameahwait, then rushed forward and threw her arms around him, weeping. It was Sacagawea, his long-lost sister.

For a moment, no one spoke. Then Cameahwait wrapped his blanket around her shoulders. The council continued, but now it felt like a family gathering. The Shoshone traded horses to the explorers, and their difficult journey could go on.

Years of endurance and hope had been rewarded. Cameahwait learned that the bonds of family can survive even the longest separation.

By August of 1805, the nights in the high valleys had already turned crisp. Cameahwait, a chief of the Lemhi Shoshone, often walked alone along the river at dusk. Unexpected Visitors

Their leaders, Captains Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, had been sent by the United States government to explore a route to the Pacific Ocean. Their boats could go no farther, and they desperately needed horses to cross the jagged Bitterroot Mountains before snow sealed the passes.

The council fire burned late that night. Some warriors despised the idea of aiding outsiders, warning that the strangers might be allied with enemy nations. Others pointed out that the explorers carried guns and goods that could help the Shoshone defend themselves and survive the coming winter. Cameahwait listened to every voice. He felt the intensity of his responsibility: to honor his ancestors, he must protect his people, yet refusing to cooperate might forfeit an opportunity that could strengthen them for years.

A Moment No One Expected

Cameahwait decided to hold a council with the explorers. Communication was slow and complicated, passing through a chain of interpreters who spoke different languages. One interpreter was a young Shoshone woman with a baby strapped to her back.

Partway through the talks, the young woman suddenly fell silent. She studied the chief's face, then sprang up, rushed to him, and embraced him, tears streaming down her cheeks. She was Sacagawea, the sister who had been taken from him so long ago.

Cameahwait drew his blanket around her shoulders. The council resumed, but its spirit had changed. The Shoshone agreed to trade horses and provide a guide, allowing the expedition to continue westward.

Years of endurance had been rewarded in a single afternoon. The reunion showed that cooperation between peoples, like the bond between a brother and sister, can grow from patience, courage, and an open heart.

Climbing Blue Hill

We start up Blue Hill
in the morning mist.
Dad goes first.
Mom holds my hand.
My little brother runs ahead
like a puppy.

The path is steep.
Tree roots grab at my boots.
The wind whispers, “Keep going.”

At the top, the sun
opens its arms.
We eat apples and gobble sandwiches.
We are tired and happy,
all together.

My Name Is Ivy

Mom named me Ivy
after the green plant
that climbs the wall.
Ivy holds on tight.
Ivy grows up and up.
That is me too.

My Grandpa's Nose

I have my grandpa's nose
and my mother's laugh.
My feet are big like Dad's.
But my ideas are all my own.

About the Poems

These are free verse poems. They do not rhyme. Poets use imagery, words that help us see and feel. Personification gives human actions to things, like wind that whispers. Each poem shows the speaker's individuality and love for family.

We leave before the sun is awake,
the morning mist a gray blanket
tucked around the valley.
Dad leads, his backpack bouncing.
My brother races ahead,
a puppy chasing every sound.

The trail climbs.
Old roots stretch across the path
like knuckles of a giant hand,
and the pines lean close to listen
to our breathing.

At the top, the sun spills gold
over every rock.
We gobble cheese sandwiches,
pass the water bottle,
and point at our small, far-off house.
From up here, we look like one family
stitched together by the wind.

Ivy

My mother named me for the vine
that climbs the old stone wall
behind Grandma's house.
It finds cracks no one else notices,
holds on through storms,
and keeps reaching.
When I'm afraid,
I remember my name.

Inheritance

I have Grandpa's crooked smile,
Mom's quick hands,
Dad's laugh that bounces off the ceiling.
But the stories in my head,
the songs I hum when no one hears,
those were born with me.

Understanding the Poems

All three poems are written in free verse, which means they have no regular rhyme or rhythm. The poets rely on imagery and figurative language instead. A metaphor, like “the morning mist a gray blanket,” compares without using like or as. Personification, such as pines that lean close to listen, gives human qualities to nature. Together, the poems celebrate family while honoring each speaker's individuality.

Climbing Blue Hill

We set out while the valley is still dreaming,
the mist a soft gray quilt
drawn up to the chin of every field.
Dad leads with a map he never opens.
Mom hums an old song from her childhood.
My brother darts ahead,
a restless sparrow testing every branch.

Higher, the trail grows stubborn.
Roots knot across the path
like the gnarled fingers of the mountain,
gripping our boots as if to ask
where we think we're going.
The pines bend their heads together,
whispering secrets we almost understand.

Then, the summit.
The sun pours itself over the rocks
like warm honey.
We gobble sandwiches, pass a dented canteen,
and search for our tiny roof below.
Up here, our family is a single shape
the wind has stitched from four different threads.

Ivy

My mother gave me the name of a climber,
the vine that scales Grandma's crumbling wall,
finding footholds in cracks
no one else would trust.
It does not ask permission to rise.
When the world feels too tall,
I whisper my name
and begin again.

Inheritance

I carry Grandpa's crooked grin,
Mom's restless hands,
Dad's laugh that rattles the windows.
They are maps of where I come from.
But the dreams that wake me early,
the colors I see when I close my eyes,
those roots reach somewhere new.

Reading Closely

These free verse poems avoid regular rhyme and meter, allowing the poets to shape lines around images and feelings. Notice the vivid imagery: sunlight like honey, mist like a quilt. Metaphors such as “a restless sparrow” describe the brother without using like or as, while personification gives roots and pines human intentions. In 1845, a young man named Henry David Thoreau made a big choice. He felt that town life in Concord, Massachusetts, was too busy and noisy. People worked all the time and never stopped to notice the world. Because of this, Henry decided to live in the woods.

He built a small cabin near Walden Pond. He used old boards and cleared away the debris around the spot. The cabin had one room, a bed, a desk, and three chairs.

Life by the Pond

Henry was a naturalist. He loved to study plants and animals. Every day, he took long walks. He might encounter a fox, a loon on the water, or ants fighting on a log. He wrote about each one in his journal.

In winter, the pond froze. Henry measured how deep the water was. His notes indicated it was over 100 feet deep in one place.

What He Learned

Henry lived at the pond for two years. Living simply made him feel free and happy. Later, he wrote a book about his life in the woods. Generations of readers have learned from it to slow down and enjoy nature.

On July 4, 1845, Henry David Thoreau moved into a one-room cabin he had built beside Walden Pond, about two miles from Concord, Massachusetts. To many of his neighbors, the decision seemed strange. Thoreau, however, had clear reasons.

Why He Left

Thoreau believed that people in town spent too much of their lives working to buy things they did not really need. He worried that they rushed past the beauty of the natural world without noticing it. As a result, he wanted to test an idea: could a person live simply and still have a rich, meaningful life?

Building a Simple Home

Thoreau borrowed an axe, cut pine trees, and bought boards from an old shed. After clearing debris from the hillside, he built a small cabin with a fireplace, a bed, a desk, and three chairs: one for solitude, two for friendship, and three for company. He grew beans in a garden, which supplied some of his food.

A Naturalist's Days

As a dedicated naturalist, Thoreau spent hours observing. He might encounter a red squirrel scolding from a branch or a loon diving and laughing on the pond. He recorded each detail in his journal, with special emphasis on how the seasons changed. During winter, he cut holes in the ice and measured the pond's depth. His careful measurements indicated that Walden was about 102 feet deep, much shallower than local legends claimed it was bottomless.

The Results

Thoreau stayed for two years and two months. His experience led to a book, Walden, published in 1854. Generations of readers have found inspiration in its spectacular descriptions of nature and its message that a simple life can be a deeply satisfying one.

On Independence Day in 1845, a twenty-seven-year-old writer named Henry David Thoreau began a personal experiment. He moved into a modest cabin he had constructed on the wooded shore of Walden Pond, roughly two miles from the bustling town of Concord, Massachusetts. Thoreau later explained his purpose plainly: he went to the woods because he wished to live deliberately, facing only the essential facts of life.

The Causes of a Bold Decision

Thoreau's choice grew from his observations of the people around him. He noticed that many of his neighbors labored endlessly to pay for larger houses, finer clothes, and possessions that brought them little lasting joy. In his view, this constant rush left people too exhausted to appreciate the natural world or to think deeply about their own lives. Consequently, he resolved to discover how little a person truly needed in order to be content.

A Cabin Built by Hand

Thoreau borrowed an axe, felled tall white pines, and purchased boards salvaged from a laborer's shanty. After clearing debris from a sunny hillside, he raised a single room about ten by fifteen feet, complete with a fireplace, a bed, a desk, and three chairs. He tracked his expenses carefully, and the house cost him just over twenty-eight dollars. A bean field nearby supplied both food and a small income.

The Eye of a Naturalist

Thoreau devoted his days to observation. On his walks he might encounter a fox crossing the snow or a loon whose eerie call echoed across the water. He placed great emphasis on precise detail, filling his journals with notes about the timing of each season's changes. In the winter of 1846, he cut holes through the ice and lowered a weighted line to measure the pond. His findings indicated a maximum depth of about one hundred two feet, disproving local claims that Walden had no bottom.

Lasting Effects

After two years and two months, Thoreau returned to town, but the experience shaped the rest of his life. In 1854 he published Walden, a book filled with spectacular descriptions of nature and sheer conviction that simplicity leads to freedom. Generations of readers, scientists, and conservationists have since been inspired by his example.

When the corner market on Elm Street closed, Rosa was upset. Now fresh vegetables were scarce in her neighborhood. Her neighbors had to take a long bus ride to buy tomatoes.

Rosa had an idea. She could grow tomatoes and sell them! But she needed land. Her yard was all concrete.

Next door lived Mr. Okafor. He was old and had a big sunny yard. Rosa took a deep breath and knocked. “Could I borrow a small piece of your yard?” she asked. “I will share my tomatoes with you.”

Mr. Okafor smiled. “That sounds like a fair loan,” he said.

Rosa used her savings to buy ten tomato plants. It was a risk. What if they did not grow? She watered them every day. She pulled weeds and tied the plants to sticks.

In July, the plants were full of red tomatoes. Rosa sold them at a small table. People were happy to buy fresh food close to home. After she paid back what she spent, she had a small profit.

Rosa learned that a small idea can help a whole neighborhood prosper.

The day the Elm Street Market closed, Rosa watched Mrs. Lee walk out carrying the last bag of onions.

Within weeks, fresh vegetables were scarce. The nearest grocery store was a forty-minute bus ride away, and many neighbors, especially older ones, could not easily make the trip.

A Plan Takes Root

Rosa, who was eleven, kept thinking about it. Her grandmother had grown tomatoes in Mexico, and Rosa had helped her every summer. What if she grew tomatoes here and sold them on the block? There was one problem: her family's yard was nothing but concrete.

Next door, Mr. Okafor had a wide, sunny backyard that had been empty since his wife passed away. Rosa practiced her speech three times before she knocked. “I'd like to rent a small corner of your yard,” she said. “I can't afford money, but I'll pay you in tomatoes.”

Mr. Okafor rubbed his chin. “A loan of land for a share of the harvest,” he said. “That's how my father farmed. Deal.”

Risk and Hard Work

Rosa emptied her savings jar, forty-two dollars from birthday gifts and dog-walking wages, and bought twelve tomato plants, soil, and stakes. Her stomach fluttered. If the plants failed, the money would be gone.

All summer she watered at sunrise, pulled weeds, and tied the vines as they grew. Mr. Okafor often came out to give advice and, Rosa noticed, to smile more than he used to.

The Harvest

By late July, the vines were heavy with red fruit. Rosa set up a folding table on the sidewalk. Neighbors lined up. By the end of August, she had earned back her forty-two dollars plus a profit of thirty more.

That evening, Rosa and Mr. Okafor planned next year's garden. This time, they would grow peppers too.

The morning the Elm Street Market closed for good, Rosa stood on the sidewalk and watched Mrs. Lee tape a hand-lettered sign to the glass: CLOSED AFTER 30 YEARS. THANK YOU, NEIGHBORS.

Within a few weeks, the effects were obvious. Fresh produce had become scarce on the block. The nearest supermarket required two buses and nearly an hour each way, a journey that was almost impossible for many of the elderly residents. Some neighbors began relying on canned food from the gas station.

An Idea Grows

Rosa could not stop thinking about the problem. Every summer, she had helped her grandmother tend a tomato patch in Oaxaca. What if she grew tomatoes here and sold them right on Elm Street? The obstacle was obvious: her family's yard was a rectangle of cracked concrete.

Next door lived Mr. Okafor, a retired bus driver whose sunny backyard had sat unused since his wife died. Rosa rehearsed her proposal until she knew it by heart. “I'd like to use a small part of your yard for a garden,” she told him. “I can't afford to pay rent, but I'll give you a share of every harvest.”

Mr. Okafor considered her for a long moment. “When I was a boy in Nigeria, my father farmed land on a loan like that,” he said. “It's an honest arrangement. Let's shake on it.”

Taking a Risk

Rosa counted her savings: forty-two dollars, earned from birthday gifts and wages for walking neighbors' dogs. She spent every cent on twelve seedlings, bags of soil, and wooden stakes. As she paid, a cold doubt crept in. If insects, heat, or her own mistakes ruined the crop, all that money would vanish.

Throughout the summer she watered at dawn, pulled weeds, and tied the climbing vines. Mr. Okafor began joining her, offering advice and, Rosa noticed, laughing more often than before.

A Neighborhood Prospers

By late July, the vines sagged with glossy red fruit. Rosa set up a card table on the sidewalk, and neighbors lined up with bags. By September, she had recovered her forty-two dollars and earned a thirty-dollar profit. More importantly, she had discovered that a single idea, combined with hard work and cooperation, could help an entire block thrive.

Most kids today use phones, tablets, or computers every day. Are these devices good for us? People have different answers.

The Good Side

Devices give us access to a lot of information. You can learn about space, animals, or history in seconds. Some games help kids practice math and reasoning. Video calls let families talk even when they live far apart.

The Bad Side

Devices also have drawbacks. Kids who use screens for many hours may not get enough exercise. Some studies cite data that too much screen time can hurt sleep. Looking at screens late at night can make it hard to fall asleep. Some kids spend less time talking face to face with friends.

A Counterpoint

Some people say all screens are bad. But that is not quite fair. Reading a science article on a tablet is very different from playing games all night.

My Claim

I believe devices can be good for us if we use them in smart ways. We should set time limits, turn screens off before bed, and go outside to play every day.

ON.body:
Smartphones, tablets, laptops, and game consoles have become part of daily life for most children. Some adults celebrate these devices as powerful learning tools, while others worry that they are harming young people. Which side does the evidence support?

Arguments for Devices

Supporters point out that devices provide instant access to information. A student curious about volcanoes can watch an eruption, read a scientist's report, and explore a 3-D model in a single afternoon. Many educational apps help students advance in math and reading at their own pace. Certain strategy games may even strengthen problem-solving and reasoning skills. Devices also help families and friends stay connected across long distances.

Arguments Against Devices

Critics, however, cite data showing real drawbacks. Health organizations report that many children spend several hours a day on screens outside of school, time that once went to outdoor play. Studies have linked screen use before bed to poorer sleep, because the bright light can trick the brain into staying alert. Some researchers also worry that heavy device use reduces face-to-face conversations, which are important for learning to understand others' feelings.

A Counterpoint Worth Considering

It is important to notice that not all screen time is equal. A careful analysis shows a big difference between video-chatting with a grandparent, researching a school project, and scrolling through videos for hours. Lumping these activities together makes the debate less useful.

My Claim

Based on this evidence, I believe electronic devices are neither entirely good nor entirely bad. Their effect depends on how they are used. Families should set clear limits, keep screens out of bedrooms at night, and make sure children balance screen activities with exercise, reading, and real conversations.
