ABOVE.body:
In just one generation, electronic devices have moved from the edges of childhood to its center. Many children now carry a smartphone, complete homework on a laptop, and relax with a game console. This rapid change has sparked a heated debate: are these devices helping young people grow, or are they quietly holding them back?

The Case for Technology

Advocates emphasize that devices offer unprecedented access to knowledge. A curious student can examine satellite images of a hurricane, read an interview with a marine biologist, or practice fractions with an app that adjusts to their level. Such tools can help learners advance at their own pace, especially when classroom time is limited. Some researchers suggest that complex strategy games may sharpen planning and reasoning. Furthermore, video calls allow children to maintain close relationships with relatives who live in other cities or even other countries.

The Case for Caution

Critics cite data that paints a more troubling picture. Surveys from health organizations indicate that many children spend several hours a day on recreational screens, often at the expense of physical activity. Studies have connected evening screen use with delayed and shorter sleep, partly because the blue-tinted light from screens can suppress the hormone that signals the body to rest. Other researchers raise concerns that constant device use may reduce face-to-face interaction, which helps children learn to read facial expressions and develop empathy.

An Important Counterpoint

A careful analysis reveals a flaw in much of this debate: it often treats all screen time as if it were identical. Yet video-chatting with a grandparent, coding a simple program, and passively scrolling through short videos for hours are fundamentally different activities with very different effects. Judging them all by the same standard leads to oversimplified conclusions.

My Claim

After weighing the evidence, I conclude that electronic devices are tools whose value depends on how they are used. The drawbacks are real, but so are the benefits. Rather than banning devices or allowing unlimited use, families and schools should teach children to use technology purposefully: setting reasonable limits, keeping devices out of bedrooms at night, choosing active and creative uses over passive ones, and protecting time for sports, books, and conversation. Thoughtful habits, not the devices themselves, will determine whether technology is good for us.

In the 1760s, there were thirteen British colonies in North America. Great Britain ruled them from far across the ocean.

The Problem

Britain needed money. So it made the colonists pay new taxes on things like paper and tea. The colonists were angry. They had no representatives in the British Parliament. No one there spoke for them. Many said, “No taxation without representation!”

The situation got worse. In 1773, colonists in Boston dumped British tea into the harbor. This was the Boston Tea Party. Britain punished Boston with strict new laws.

Looking for Solutions

The colonies formed committees to share news and plans. In 1774, leaders met at a big meeting called a convention. They held a long debate about how to resolve the problem. Some wanted to stay with Britain. Others wanted to be free.

In 1775, fighting began. George Washington led the colonial army.

The Answer

In 1776, Thomas Jefferson wrote a proposal called the Declaration of Independence. The colonies agreed to it. They would form a new union: the United States of America.

By the 1760s, about two million people lived in Britain's thirteen American colonies. For many years, the colonies had mostly governed their own affairs. Then the relationship began to change.

The Problem: Taxes Without a Voice

After a costly war, Britain needed money, so Parliament passed new taxes on the colonies, including the Stamp Act of 1765 and later a tax on tea. The colonists objected not only to the cost but also to the principle. They elected no representatives to Parliament, so they had no voice in the laws that affected them. “No taxation without representation” became their rallying cry.

The Situation Grows Worse

Protests spread. In 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston, killing five people. In 1773, colonists disguised themselves and dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbor. Britain responded by closing the harbor and limiting town meetings in Massachusetts.

Searching for a Solution

To coordinate their response, the colonies formed committees of correspondence that carried news between towns. In 1774, delegates from twelve colonies gathered at a convention in Philadelphia called the First Continental Congress. They hoped to resolve the crisis peacefully and sent a petition to the king. The king rejected it.

From Debate to Independence

In April 1775, fighting broke out at Lexington and Concord. The Second Continental Congress named George Washington commander of the army. After a long debate, Congress approved a proposal for independence. On July 4, 1776, it adopted the Declaration of Independence, written mainly by Thomas Jefferson.

The declaration was only the beginning. Years of war followed, but the colonies had chosen a new solution: to form a union of their own.

ABOVE.body:
In the middle of the eighteenth century, Britain's thirteen colonies along the Atlantic coast enjoyed considerable freedom. Their own assemblies passed most local laws, and London rarely interfered. That situation changed dramatically after 1763.

The Problem: Taxation Without Representation

The French and Indian War had left Britain deeply in debt, and Parliament concluded that the colonies should help pay for their own defense. It imposed a series of taxes, including the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed printed materials, and duties on imported goods such as tea. Colonists protested that, as British subjects, they could be taxed only by representatives they had elected. Because they had no seats in Parliament, the taxes seemed to violate their fundamental rights.

Escalating Conflict

Resistance took many forms, from boycotts of British goods to angry demonstrations. Tensions exploded in 1770, when soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston, killing five colonists. Three years later, protesters dumped hundreds of chests of tea into Boston Harbor. Parliament retaliated with harsh measures that closed the port and restricted self-government in Massachusetts, which convinced many colonists that their liberties were in danger.

Organizing a Response

To coordinate resistance, colonial leaders created committees of correspondence that spread information quickly from town to town. In 1774, delegates from twelve colonies assembled in Philadelphia for the First Continental Congress. This convention attempted to resolve the dispute peacefully by petitioning King George III to restore their rights. The king refused to consider their complaints.

The Solution: Independence

When fighting erupted at Lexington and Concord in 1775, the Second Continental Congress appointed George Washington to command a new Continental Army. Throughout the following year, delegates engaged in intense debate. Some still hoped for reconciliation, while others argued that independence was the only option. In June 1776, a proposal for independence was formally introduced, and a committee asked Thomas Jefferson to draft a declaration explaining the colonies' reasons. On July 4, 1776, Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence.

The colonists had chosen a bold solution to their problem. Instead of remaining unrepresented subjects, they would build a new union governed by their own elected representatives, though securing that independence would require years of war.

Long ago in China, a poor mother wove cloth to sell. One year she wove a brocade, a cloth with pictures in silk thread. It showed a beautiful house, a garden, and a river. It took her three years to finish.

The day she finished, a strong wind blew. It grabbed the brocade and carried it far away. The mother was so sad that she became sick.

Her youngest son, Li, said, “I will find it, Mother.”

Li walked for days. He met an old woman by a stone horse. She gave him guidance. “Fairies on Sun Mountain took the brocade,” she said. “To get there, you must cross a valley of fire and an icy sea. Do not be afraid.”

Li was brave. He walked through the fire. He swam through the icy water. At last, he climbed the steep mountain. The fairies were copying the beautiful brocade. They gave it back to him with gratitude for letting them learn from it.

Li ran home. He opened the brocade, and the picture became real! His mother was well again. Courage and love had saved them.

Long ago, at the foot of a mountain in southern China, there lived a widow and her three sons. The widow was a gifted weaver, and she sold her brocades to buy rice.

One day she saw a painting of a splendid house with gardens and fields, and she decided to weave it. For three years she worked day and night. Her tears fell on the threads and became a sparkling river. Her blood from pricked fingers became a scarlet sun.

The brocade was finally finished. But as she carried it outside to admire it in the light, a fierce wind snatched it and swept it over the mountains. The widow grew so sad that she fell ill.

The Journey

The two older sons set out to find the brocade, but when an old woman told them about the dangers ahead, they took her gold and ran away. The youngest son, Le Jé, set out next.

The old woman offered him the same guidance. “The fairies of Sun Mountain have taken it. You must ride through a valley of flames and cross a freezing sea. If you cry out once, you will be lost.” Le Jé did not hesitate.

He rode through scorching fire without a sound. He crossed the icy sea, his body numb with cold, assuring himself that his mother needed him. At last, he reached a palace where fairies were weaving copies of his mother's work. They thanked him with gratitude for the chance to learn from it and returned the brocade.

The Outcome

When Le Jé unrolled the brocade before his mother, it grew larger and larger until the house, gardens, and river became real. His mother recovered. The lesson was clear: perseverance and love bring rewards that greed never can.

In a village beneath tall green mountains in southern China, there once lived a widow who supported her three sons by weaving brocades, glimmering silk cloths decorated with intricate scenes.

One afternoon at the market, she noticed a painting of a magnificent house surrounded by orchards, flowering gardens, and golden fields. Gazing at it, she felt a longing she had never known. She bought the painting with her last coins and resolved to weave the scene herself. For three years she labored by firelight. When her eyes grew tired, her tears fell upon the cloth and became a shimmering stream. When her fingers bled, the drops became a crimson sun rising over the hills.

At last the brocade was complete. She carried it into the courtyard to admire it in the daylight, but a violent gust detected the treasure, tore it from her hands, and carried it over the ridge. Heartbroken, the widow took to her bed.

Three Brothers, Three Choices

The eldest son set out in pursuit. At a crossroads he met an old woman seated beside a stone horse. She explained that the fairies of Sun Mountain had taken the brocade and that the road there crossed a valley of flames and a frozen sea. Then she offered him a box of gold if he preferred to turn back. He took the gold and never returned home. The middle son made the same choice.

When the youngest son, Le Jé, reached the crossroads, he refused the gold. The old woman's guidance was stern: “If you utter a single cry of pain, you will be swept away.” Le Jé rode through roaring flames in silence. He crossed the icy sea, assuring himself with every stroke that his mother was waiting. Emerging on the far shore, he climbed to a palace where fairies sat copying his mother's design. Out of gratitude for the chance to learn from such beauty, they returned the cloth.

The Outcome

When Le Jé spread the brocade before his mother, it stretched across the valley until every orchard and stream became real. His mother's health returned, while the greedy brothers, having wasted their previous fortune, wandered home as beggars. The tale reminds listeners that devotion and perseverance, not easy rewards, lead to lasting happiness.

A Simple Plan

My brother Sam had a simple plan,
to change the world the best he can.
Not with a crown, not with a sword,
just one kind act he could afford.

He helped a neighbor rake her leaves,
he found a lost cat in the trees,
he memorized a poem to read
to kids at school who were in need.

I said, “Your plan is way too small.”
He said, “Small things add up for all.”
So I joined in, and day by day,
we gave our kindness away.

One Step

One step,
one smile,
one hand held out.
That's what
changing the world
is all about.

About the Poems

The first poem is a narrative poem. It tells a story. It uses rhyme, like plan and can. The second poem is free verse. It is short and does not follow a pattern. Both poems use repetition, such as the word one, to show their message. Helping others gives a feeling of satisfaction.

A Simple Plan

My brother Sam was ten years old
and ambitious as a king;
he said, “I'm going to change the world,”
and didn't own a thing.

No army and no fancy speech,
no money in the bank,
just two hands and a simple plan
and sneakers worn and blank.

He shoveled snow for Mrs. Grey,
who couldn't leave her door;
he memorized the bus routes
to guide new kids once more.

I laughed at him. I said, “That's it?
That's how you'll change the earth?”
He shrugged and said, “Each little thing
has more than what it's worth.”

That winter, when the wind blew hard
and I shuddered in the cold,
I saw a line of neighbors' walks
he'd cleared, both young and old.

So now we work as two, not one,
we rake, we read, we mend;
the satisfaction that we feel
is worth it in the end.

If Not Now

If not now, when?
If not you, who?
The world is waiting
for what you will do.
A hand.
A word.
A door held wide.
Begin today.
Step outside.

Thinking About the Poems

A Simple Plan

My brother Sam, at ten years old,
announced at dinner, bright and bold,
“I'm going to change the world,” he said.
I laughed so hard I bumped my head.

He had no fortune, had no fame,
no famous friends who knew his name,
just ambitious eyes and empty hands
and stubborn, quiet, simple plans.

He shoveled out old Mrs. Grey,
whose porch was snowed in every day;
he memorized each city route
to guide new students, lost, about.

He read aloud to kids at three
who couldn't read as well as he;
he fixed the fence, he fed the cat,
he smiled and asked for nothing back.

“Is that your plan?” I mocked one night.
“You'll never set the world aright.”
He answered, calm as falling snow,
“A thousand candles start one glow.”

That January, bitter, gray,
I shuddered on my walk one day,
and saw a path he'd cleared for miles,
and neighbors' doors, and neighbors' smiles.

Now side by side, we rake and mend,
we read, we build, we help, we lend;
the satisfaction, warm and true,
is something money can't buy you.

If Not Now

If not now, then when?
If not you, then who?
The world is not a mountain
to be moved by giants.
It is a garden
tended by small hands.
A kind word.
A borrowed coat.
A door held open in the rain.
If not now, then when?
Begin.

Reading the Poems

“A Simple Plan” is a narrative poem: it tells a story with a beginning, middle, and end, using rhyming couplets and regular stanzas. “If Not Now” is free verse, without a fixed rhyme or rhythm. Both use repetition to reinforce meaning. In the first poem, the speaker's change from mockery to partnership shows the power of example. In the second, the repeated questions challenge readers directly. Together, they suggest that extraordinary change begins with ordinary people willing to act.

Diego did not want to go to Argentina. His soccer team in New York had a summer tournament. “Why do I have to visit Buenos Aires?” he blurted at dinner.

“To meet your grandfather's family,” Mom said.

On the plane, Diego was critical of everything. The food was bad. The trip was long.

In Buenos Aires, his cousin Lucía showed him the city. They ate empanadas, little pies filled with meat. Diego wanted to say they were not as good as pizza. But he took a bite. They were delicious!

That night, there was music in the street. People danced the tango. Diego watched a man play a small accordion. He forgot to be grumpy.

The next day, Lucía took him to a park. Kids were playing soccer! Diego joined in. He scored a goal, and a boy came over to congratulate him.

Diego saw that Buenos Aires was a lot like New York. Both cities were busy and full of music and soccer.

At the end of the trip, Diego felt a new appreciation for his family's home. “Can we come back next summer?” he asked.

“Two weeks in Argentina?” Diego blurted. “But the summer tournament starts on the fifteenth!”

His mother calmly set down her fork. “Your great-aunt Rosa is turning eighty. The whole family will be in Buenos Aires.”

Diego sulked all the way to the airport. On the long flight, he was critical of everything: the cramped seats, the strange movies, the rubbery chicken.

New Flavors

In Buenos Aires, his cousin Lucía met them with a wide grin. That afternoon she took Diego to a bakery and handed him an empanada. He was about to say that nothing beat New York pizza, but one bite of the flaky crust and spiced beef contradicted him completely. He ate three.

New Sounds

That evening, in the old neighborhood of San Telmo, couples danced the tango in the plaza while a musician squeezed a bandoneón, a kind of accordion. Diego was surprised to find himself tapping his foot.

A Familiar Game

The next morning Lucía led him to a park where kids were playing a fast pickup soccer game. Diego hesitated, but they waved him in. When he scored with a left-footed shot, a tall boy ran over to congratulate him. “¡Golazo!” he shouted.

A Misunderstanding

At dinner Diego tried complimenting his great-aunt in Spanish, but he mixed up two words and accidentally said her soup was “embarrassed.” The table burst into laughter, and Aunt Rosa laughed loudest of all. The misunderstanding made everyone feel closer.

Going Home

By the end of the trip, Diego realized that Buenos Aires and New York had a lot in common: crowded streets, late dinners, music everywhere, and a deep love of soccer. On the plane home, he felt a new appreciation for his family's cultural roots. “Next summer,” he told his mother, “let's stay longer.”

On the night of April 20, 2010, an explosion tore through the Deepwater Horizon, an oil-drilling platform in the Gulf of Mexico. Eleven workers lost their lives, and two days later the burning platform sank. Far below, a broken well on the seafloor began releasing oil into the ocean. Over the following months, millions of barrels poured into the Gulf. Facing this disaster, thousands of people with very different skills came together.

Engineers Versus the Deep

The damaged well sat about a mile beneath the surface, where the water is pitch-dark and the pressure would crush a human diver. Engineers controlled remotely operated robots to work at that depth. Their first attempts to stop the leak failed, but they kept trying new techniques. On July 15, after 87 days, a specially designed cap finally sealed the well.

Containing the Oil

Meanwhile, crews fought the oil at the surface. Workers laid out hundreds of miles of floating barriers called booms to protect beaches and marshes. Skimmer boats scooped oil off the water, and firefighting crews performed controlled burns to remove thick patches.

Rescuing Wildlife

The oil coated pelicans, sea turtles, and other animals. Dedicated veterinarians and volunteers set up rescue centers where they carefully washed oiled birds with dish soap, rinsed them, and helped them recover before releasing them into clean areas.

Lessons in Teamwork

Scientists also studied the spill's effects on the Gulf's food chain, and some researchers developed new materials designed to mimic the way certain natural fibers absorb oil. The response showed that when people collaborate and remain flexible, they can overcome even an enormous obstacle.

Shortly before ten o'clock on the night of April 20, 2010, natural gas surged up a well beneath the Deepwater Horizon drilling platform in the Gulf of Mexico and ignited. The explosion killed eleven workers, and after burning for two days, the enormous structure sank. Nearly a mile below the surface, the damaged wellhead began releasing oil into the sea. By the time the leak was stopped, roughly four million barrels had escaped, making it one of the largest marine oil spills in history. The response would require an extraordinary range of people working together.

The Engineering Challenge

The well's location created a formidable obstacle. At that depth there is no sunlight, the water is near freezing, and the pressure would crush any diver. Engineers therefore operated remotely controlled underwater robots, guiding them by video from ships above. Several techniques failed, including an attempt to lower a giant containment dome that clogged with icy crystals. Engineers remained flexible, redesigning their tools after every setback. On July 15, after 87 days, a tightly fitted capping stack finally stopped the flow.

Defending the Coast

At the surface, a different battle unfolded. Crews deployed hundreds of miles of floating booms to keep oil away from fragile marshes and beaches. Skimmer vessels gathered oil from the water, while trained crews conducted controlled burns of the thickest slicks. Communities along the coast organized volunteers to monitor shorelines and report new contamination.

Caring for Wildlife

Oil is deadly to animals because it destroys the waterproofing of feathers and fur and can be swallowed during cleaning. Dedicated veterinarians and wildlife specialists established rehabilitation centers where teams washed each oiled bird with dish detergent, rinsed it with warm water, and allowed it to regain strength before release.

Science and Innovation

Researchers studied how the oil affected plankton, fish, and the larger food web. Some scientists began developing artificial materials that mimic the oil-absorbing function of certain natural fibers, aiming to improve future cleanups.

The Gulf spill caused lasting harm, yet the response demonstrated a powerful truth: when people with different expertise collaborate, adapt, and persist, they can confront even the most overwhelming environmental crisis.

About 500 years ago, the Inca Empire stretched along the mountains of South America. The Inca built roads, cities, and farms. But they did not use a written alphabet. So how did they keep records?

The Quipu

The Inca used quipus. A quipu is a main cord with many strings hanging from it. Each string had knots. The colors of the strings and the places of the knots had meaning.

What We Know

An archaeologist digs up objects from the past. A historian studies old records. They found that many quipus show numbers. A knot near the bottom stood for ones. Knots higher up stood for tens and hundreds. Officials used quipus to count people, llamas, and crops.

What We Still Wonder

Today about 1,000 quipus are preserved. Some are intact. Others are just fragments. Some experts think quipus also told stories or recorded names. They are trying to reconstruct how this worked.

My Claim

I believe quipus were more than math tools. They were a smart way to share many kinds of information. Scientists should keep studying them.

ON.body:
The Inca Empire, which flourished in the Andes Mountains of South America during the 1400s and early 1500s, governed millions of people across thousands of miles. Its builders created stone cities and a road network longer than 20,000 miles. Yet the Inca had no written alphabet. Instead, they relied on an ingenious device: the quipu.

Strings That Speak

A quipu is made of a main cord with dozens or even hundreds of thinner strings hanging from it. These strings, made of cotton or llama and alpaca wool, were dyed different colors and tied with different types of knots. Specially trained officials called quipucamayocs created and read them.

The Case for Numbers

In the early 1900s, researchers discovered that many quipus use a base-ten system, like ours. Clusters of knots near the bottom of a string represent ones, the next group represents tens, then hundreds, and so on. Historians who compared quipus with early Spanish records concluded that officials used them to track population, taxes, crops, and herds.

The Case for Language

However, not every quipu fits this pattern. Some contain unusual knots and color combinations that do not seem to represent numbers. Spanish writers from that era reported that quipu keepers could recite histories, laws, and even poems from their cords. Some modern researchers believe the strings recorded names of people and places.

My Claim

About a thousand quipus are preserved today, though many are only fragments. An archaeologist working with them faces a puzzle with missing pieces. Even so, I believe the evidence shows that quipus were more than calculators. They were likely a complete system of communication, and continuing research may one day allow scholars to reconstruct their full meaning.

ABOVE.body:
At its height in the early 1500s, the Inca Empire stretched more than 2,500 miles along the Andes Mountains, governing perhaps ten million people. Inca engineers built terraced farms on steep slopes, stone cities that have withstood centuries of earthquakes, and a road system exceeding 20,000 miles. Remarkably, the empire accomplished all this without a written alphabet. Its records were stored instead in knotted strings called quipus, and their exact purpose remains one of history's great unsolved questions.

Anatomy of a Quipu

A quipu consists of a primary cord from which hang pendant strings, sometimes numbering in the hundreds, along with smaller subsidiary strings. The cords were spun from cotton or camelid fiber, dyed in a range of colors, and tied with several distinct kinds of knots. Trained specialists known as quipucamayocs were responsible for creating, storing, and interpreting them.

The Numerical Interpretation

In 1912, a researcher demonstrated that many quipus encode numbers using a base-ten positional system. Knots clustered near the end of a string represent ones, the next cluster tens, then hundreds, and so forth. When historians compared quipus with records made by Spanish officials shortly after the conquest, the totals often matched, confirming that the cords tracked census figures, tribute payments, harvests, and livestock.

The Linguistic Interpretation

Yet roughly a third of surviving quipus do not fit the numerical pattern. Their knot types, colors, and string arrangements appear too irregular to be simple arithmetic. Spanish chroniclers of the era described quipucamayocs reciting genealogies, historical events, and laws from their cords. Some modern scholars have identified patterns that may represent names of villages or family groups, suggesting the strings could record words as well as numbers.

Weighing the Evidence

Today about a thousand quipus are preserved in museums and private collections. Many are intact, but others survive only as remnants, and few come with information about where they were found. Despite these limitations, the combined evidence leads me to a clear claim: quipus were not merely accounting tools but a flexible information system capable of storing both numerical and narrative records. If archaeologists and historians continue to collaborate, comparing quipus with one another and with colonial documents, they may eventually reconstruct the complete language of the knots.

Frederick Douglass was born into slavery on Maryland's Eastern Shore around 1818. He never knew his exact birthday, and he saw his mother only a few times, always at night. From his earliest years, he experienced the cruelty of a system that treated human beings as property and kept them in unequal, brutal conditions.

The Power of Reading

At about age eight, Frederick was sent to Baltimore to work in the home of Hugh and Sophia Auld. Sophia began teaching him the alphabet until her husband angrily forbade it, warning that reading would make Frederick unfit to be enslaved. Frederick realized that literacy was a path to freedom. He sought lessons from neighborhood boys, trading bread for their help, and secretly practiced writing by copying letters he saw on wooden planks at the shipyard.

The Road North

In September 1838, Frederick disguised himself as a free sailor and boarded a northbound train with borrowed papers. His heart pounded with fear and anticipation at every station. Within a day he reached New York, a free man.

A Voice That Would Not Be Silenced

In 1841, at a meeting in Massachusetts, Frederick was asked to describe his life. Though nervous and normally reserved in front of strangers, he spoke with such power that the abolitionists hired him as a lecturer. He became one of the most outspoken voices against slavery, publishing an autobiography in 1845 and later founding a newspaper. He argued that every person was entitled to liberty and that no one could remain neutral in the face of such injustice.

I believe Douglass's life proves that education and courage are powerful weapons. He chose to defy those who wanted him silent, and his words helped change a nation.

Frederick Douglass, born around 1818 on Maryland's Eastern Shore, began life with almost nothing: no record of his birthday, little contact with his mother, and no legal rights. Like millions of enslaved people, he was considered property, subjected to hunger, exhausting labor, and violence under a profoundly unequal system. That he rose to become one of the most influential Americans of the nineteenth century is a testament to his extraordinary determination.

Literacy as Liberation

Around the age of eight, Frederick was sent to Baltimore to serve the household of Hugh and Sophia Auld. Sophia, at first, began teaching him to read, but her husband abruptly forbade the lessons, declaring that education would make an enslaved boy discontented. Frederick later wrote that this moment revealed to him the pathway from slavery to freedom. He sought instruction wherever he could, exchanging bread with hungry neighborhood boys for reading lessons and teaching himself to write by imitating letters marked on timber in the shipyards. Reading newspapers and speeches, he became convinced that he was entitled to the same liberty as anyone else.

A Daring Escape

In September 1838, carrying papers borrowed from a free Black sailor and dressed in a sailor's uniform, Frederick boarded a train heading north. Every inspection filled him with dread and anticipation, but within twenty-four hours he stepped off in New York as a free man.

An Unforgettable Voice

Three years later, at an antislavery convention on the island of Nantucket, Douglass was invited to speak. Despite feeling nervous and somewhat reserved, he described his experiences so vividly that the audience was transfixed. Abolitionist leaders immediately recruited him as a lecturer. Douglass became an outspoken critic of slavery, publishing his autobiography in 1845, which exposed the system's cruelty in his own words, and later establishing an antislavery newspaper. He insisted that Americans could not remain neutral while millions were enslaved.

The Author's View

To me, Douglass's greatest achievement was not his escape but his decision to defy silence. He could have lived quietly in freedom. Instead, he risked recapture to tell the truth publicly, proving that a single courageous voice, sharpened by education, can challenge the conscience of an entire nation.

CHARACTERS:
MAYA, an inquisitive student
JON, the class science expert
PRIYA, a careful organizer
MR. COLE, their teacher

SETTING: A fifth-grade classroom early in the morning. A glass terrarium with branches and a heat lamp stands near the window.

(MAYA enters first, hangs up her backpack, and peers into the terrarium. She freezes.)

MAYA: Everyone! Brownie's gone!

(JON and PRIYA rush over.)

JON: (perplexed) That's impossible. Chameleons can't open lids.

PRIYA: (crossing her arms, suspicious) Jon, you were on feeding duty yesterday. Are you sure you closed it?

JON: (hurt) Of course I'm sure! You always assume it's my fault.

MR. COLE: (entering) Hold on. Accusations won't find Brownie. Evidence will. What do we know?

MAYA: (examining the lid closely) Look! The latch is bent. There's a gap at this corner, just wide enough for a small chameleon.

PRIYA: (reconsidering) So maybe it wasn't Jon. Maybe the latch broke.

JON: Chameleons need warmth. When the heat lamp turned off last night, Brownie probably went looking for somewhere warm.

MR. COLE: Good reasoning. Where's the warmest spot in the room right now?

MAYA: The windowsill. The sun hits it every morning.

(They tiptoe toward the window, where a potted fern sits in a beam of sunlight.)

PRIYA: I don't see anything.

JON: Be precise. Look for a curled tail, or eyes that move separately.

(MAYA leans close. One leaf seems to blink.)

MAYA: (astounded) He's right there! He's turned exactly the color of the fern!

MR. COLE: Excellent detective work. You interpreted the clues instead of guessing.

PRIYA: (turning to JON) I'm sorry I blamed you. I should have looked at the evidence first.

JON: (smiling) Apology accepted. Now let's fix that latch together.

THE END

CHARACTERS:
MAYA, an inquisitive student who notices details
JON, the class science expert, quick to defend himself
PRIYA, an organized student who likes rules
MR. COLE, their calm and patient teacher

SETTING: A fifth-grade science classroom at 7:45 a.m. A large glass terrarium, complete with twisting branches, a water dish, and a heat lamp, stands near a sunny window.

(MAYA enters, hangs her backpack on a hook, and wanders to the terrarium. She stops, leans closer, and gasps.)

MAYA: Everyone, come quick! Brownie isn't in here!

(JON and PRIYA hurry over.)

JON: (perplexed, scanning every branch) He has to be. Chameleons blend in. Maybe he's just camouflaged.

PRIYA: (after checking carefully, then narrowing her eyes, suspicious) He's not. Jon, you had feeding duty yesterday afternoon. Did you latch the lid?

JON: (defensively) Yes! Why does everything that goes wrong in this room become my fault?

MR. COLE: (setting down his coffee) Let's pause. Accusations feel satisfying, but they rarely solve mysteries. Evidence does. What can we observe?

MAYA: (running her finger along the lid) This latch is bent upward. There's a gap in the corner about two centimeters wide.

PRIYA: (slowly, beginning to reconsider) Brownie could squeeze through that. So the latch failed, not Jon.

JON: (calming down) And here's another clue: the heat lamp is on a timer. It switches off at night. Chameleons are cold-blooded, so Brownie would have searched for warmth.

MR. COLE: Then let's interpret what the room is telling us. Where would warmth be right now?

MAYA: The windowsill. Morning sunlight hits it first.

(They creep toward a potted fern bathed in sunlight.)

PRIYA: I still don't see him.

JON: We need to be precise. Look for a coiled tail, or eyes that swivel separately.

(A long pause. Then one “leaf” rotates an eye toward them.)

MAYA: (astounded) There! He's matched the fern so perfectly he's practically invisible!

MR. COLE: Brilliant. You combined observation, scientific knowledge, and teamwork. That is exactly how real scientists work.

PRIYA: (turning to JON, sincerely) I owe you an apology. I jumped to a conclusion because it was easy, not because it was true.

JON: (grinning) Apology accepted. Next time, let's investigate before we accuse. Now, who wants to help me repair this latch?

THE END

articles.title: How Do I Hold the Summer?

BELOW.body:
How Do I Hold the Summer?

How do I hold the summer
when the summer wants to go?
The sun is soft and golden,
the days are long and slow.

I'll put the beach inside a jar,
the waves inside a shell,
the smell of grass inside a book,
the ice cream bell as well.

The trees will soon be barren,
the wind will start to blow,
but I will hold the summer
in my heart through winter snow.

The Fly

A fly flits fast,
a buzzing bead,
she zips and zooms
with speedy speed.
Her wings are glass,
her eyes are stars,
she lands on jam
in sticky jars.

About the Poems

The first poem is a lyric poem. It shares the speaker's feelings. Each group of lines is a stanza. The second poem uses alliteration, words that start with the same sound, like fly flits fast. Both poems use meaningful words to help us see and feel.

ON.body:
How Do I Hold the Summer?

How do I hold the summer
as it slips between my hands,
like water from the river,
like the soft and shifting sands?

I'll fold the sunset in a drawer,
the crickets in a box,
the salty breeze inside a jar
beside my sandy socks.

I'll press a daisy in a book
to keep its yellow light,
and save the laughter of my friends
for some long winter night.

The fields will soon be barren,
the geese will fly away,
but summer lives in what I keep,
and memories can stay.

The Fly

A fly, a flicker, flits and flies,
a shiny speck of black,
she zigzags on her zippy wings
and never once looks back.

Her eyes are mirrors, many-faced,
her legs are tiny threads,
she dances on the window glass
and buzzes round our heads.

Notes on the Poems

“How Do I Hold the Summer?” is a lyric poem, a short poem that expresses the speaker's personal feelings. It is organized into stanzas of four lines with a steady meter. The speaker uses similes, such as comparing summer to water slipping through hands, to show how hard it is to keep something wonderful from ending. “The Fly” uses alliteration, the repetition of beginning sounds, as in “flicker, flits and flies,” to imitate the quick, buzzing movement of the insect. Each poem shows how a poet's expression can make ordinary experiences feel meaningful.

ABOVE.body:
How Do I Hold the Summer?

How do I hold the summer
when it slides between my hands
like river water, warm and quick,
like evening's sinking sands?

I'll fold the sunset, peach and plum,
and tuck it in a drawer;
I'll cage the crickets' midnight song
beside the cellar door.

I'll bottle up the salted breeze,
the gulls, the green-gold spray,
and press the last wild daisy flat
to keep its light at bay.

The maples, plumes of crimson flame,
will shed their burning crowns;
the fields will lie down barren, brown,
beneath November's gowns.

But I have learned a quiet trick:
the heart's a deeper jar;
what's loved is never truly lost,
however gone, or far.

The Fly

A flicker, flitting, flashing fly,
a speck of polished jet,
she zigzags through the kitchen air,
not finished with us yet.

Her eyes are many-windowed domes,
her wings are slips of glass;
she pirouettes on window panes
and watches seasons pass.

She tastes the jam with tiny feet,
she scorns our swatting hands,
a dancer in a buzzing gown
who never understands.

Reading the Poems Closely

“How Do I Hold the Summer?” is a lyric poem: through regular four-line stanzas and a steady meter, the speaker expresses a personal longing to preserve the season's beauty. Vivid similes and metaphors, such as autumn maples described as plumes of flame, intensify the sense of loss as summer fades. Yet the final stanza transforms that sadness into hope: the heart becomes “a deeper jar” where meaningful memories endure. “The Fly,” by contrast, is playful. Its alliteration, like “flicker, flitting, flashing fly,” imitates the insect's darting motion, while metaphors turn an ordinary pest into a dancer. Together, the poems show how a poet's expression can transform both the grand and the tiny into something worth noticing.

Long ago, most people believed that Earth stood still. They thought the Sun, the Moon, and the stars all moved around Earth. Ideas about Earth have changed a lot since then.

A New Idea

In 1543, an astronomer named Nicolaus Copernicus shared a new idea. He said that Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun. Many people did not believe him at first.

A Closer Look

About 60 years later, Galileo Galilei used a telescope. He saw moons going around Jupiter. This showed that not everything moves around Earth. His astronomical observations helped prove Copernicus right.

Measuring Earth

Scientists also wanted to know Earth's size. They used math and careful calculation. Today we know Earth's diameter is approximately 12,700 kilometers.

Looking from Above

Later, people sent weather balloons and airplanes high into the sky. Now satellites circle Earth. They take pictures and collect data about clouds, oceans, and air.

Each new tool helped people understand our planet better. Our view of Earth keeps changing as science grows.

For thousands of years, people looked at the sky and drew a reasonable conclusion: Earth must be standing still. After all, the Sun seemed to rise in the east and set in the west, and the stars appeared to wheel across the night. Most scholars believed Earth sat at the center of the universe, surrounded by the Sun, Moon, and planets.

A Bold Proposal

In 1543, the Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus published a book with a startling idea. He argued that the Sun, not Earth, was at the center, and that Earth was simply one planet in orbit around it. Because his idea contradicted what people could see and what many authorities taught, it was slow to be accepted.

Evidence Through a Lens

In 1610, Galileo Galilei pointed a telescope at the sky and made a series of astronomical discoveries. He saw four moons circling Jupiter, proof that not everything revolved around Earth. He also observed that Venus showed phases like the Moon, which fit Copernicus's model far better than the old one.

Measuring Our Planet

Scientists developed criteria for testing ideas: a good explanation had to match careful observations and accurate calculation. Using geometry, they measured Earth with increasing precision. Today we know its diameter is approximately 12,742 kilometers.

A View from Above

In the 1800s and 1900s, weather balloons and airplanes carried instruments high into the atmosphere. Since 1957, satellites have orbited Earth, photographing storms and measuring oceans and ice.

Each new instrument has allowed scientists to evaluate old ideas and replace them with better ones. Our understanding of Earth has grown because people kept asking questions and testing the answers.

ABOVE.body:
For most of human history, the evidence of our senses pointed to a single conclusion: Earth is motionless, and the heavens revolve around it. Each day the Sun crossed the sky from east to west, and each night the stars turned in slow, predictable circles. Ancient Greek thinkers, most influentially Ptolemy in the second century, organized these observations into an elaborate model in which the Sun, Moon, and planets traveled around a stationary Earth on nested spheres. For roughly fourteen centuries, this geocentric model dominated scientific thought.

A Revolutionary Proposal

In 1543, Nicolaus Copernicus published a book proposing a heliocentric model, with the Sun at the center and Earth as one of several planets in orbit around it. His system explained puzzling planetary motions more simply, yet it challenged both common sense and established authority. Many scholars rejected it, and for decades it remained a controversial hypothesis.

The Telescope Provides Evidence

The decisive evidence came from a new instrument. In 1610, Galileo Galilei turned an improved telescope toward the night sky and recorded a series of astonishing astronomical observations. He discovered four moons orbiting Jupiter, demonstrating that not every celestial body circles Earth. He also documented the full cycle of phases of Venus, a pattern that the geocentric model could not explain but the heliocentric model predicted.

The Role of Measurement

As science matured, researchers adopted stricter criteria for accepting an idea: it must agree with precise observation and survive mathematical calculation. Using geometry and, later, satellite measurements, scientists determined that Earth's diameter is approximately 12,742 kilometers and that the planet bulges slightly at the equator.

New Perspectives from Above

The nineteenth and twentieth centuries brought tools that let scientists study Earth itself from great heights. Weather balloons carried instruments into the upper atmosphere, aircraft photographed landscapes, and, beginning in 1957, artificial satellites began circling the planet. Today, satellites continuously monitor hurricanes, sea levels, and polar ice, gathering data no ground-based observer could collect.

The history of these changing views reveals the essential nature of science: no idea is accepted simply because it is familiar. Each generation must evaluate earlier conclusions against new evidence, and with every improved instrument, our picture of Earth becomes more accurate.

articles.title: The Day the Rollets Got Their Moxie Back

BELOW.body:
It was 1934 in New York City. Times were hard. Papa had lost his job at the factory. Mama sewed clothes late at night to earn a little money. The Rollet family was sad and worried.

Their big brother, Joe, had joined a government work program. He planted trees in the mountains. Every week, he sent money home and a letter. “Don't lose your moxie!” he always wrote. Moxie means courage and spirit.

Twelve-year-old Ellie read the letter out loud. “We have lost our moxie,” she said. “Papa never smiles anymore.”

Her little sister, Bea, had an idea. “Let's put on a talent show for the building!”

Ellie was not sure. “People will assume we are silly,” she said.

But Bea did not give up. The sisters asked their neighbors to join. Mrs. Klein played the violin. The Russo boys did a funny dance. Bea sang, and Ellie told jokes.

On Saturday night, everyone came to the roof. They laughed and clapped. Even Papa laughed.

The Rollets still did not have much money. But they had their moxie back.

ON.body:
In the winter of 1934, the Great Depression had settled over New York City like a gray blanket. Papa Rollet had lost his job at the button factory eight months earlier. Mama sewed shirts by lamplight for a few cents each. At dinner, nobody talked much anymore.

Letters from the Mountains

The family's oldest son, Joe, had enlisted in the Civilian Conservation Corps, a government work program. Every week he mailed most of his wages home along with a cheerful letter. Each one ended the same way: Don't lose your moxie! Moxie was Joe's word for courage and spirit.

Twelve-year-old Ellie read the latest letter aloud, then folded it with a sigh. “Joe would be disappointed,” she said. “We've obviously lost every bit of moxie we had.”

A Risky Idea

Her younger sister, Bea, jumped up. “Then let's find it! We'll put on a talent show for the whole building, right on the roof.”

Ellie frowned. “People are hungry, Bea. They'll think we're being foolish. And I can't guarantee anyone will come.”

“Joe wouldn't call that a reason to quit,” Bea said.

Building the Show

For two weeks, the sisters knocked on every door. Mrs. Klein agreed to play violin. The Russo twins worked up a comedy act. Even Mama agreed to sing. Ellie, who had always been shy, nominated herself as the announcer.

The Night of the Show

On Saturday, neighbors climbed to the roof carrying blankets and chairs. As the Russo twins tripped over each other in their silly routine, a sound rang out that Ellie had not heard in months: Papa's deep, rumbling laugh.

That night Ellie wrote to Joe. We still don't have much money, she wrote, but you'll be glad to know we found our moxie.

ABOVE.body:
By the winter of 1934, the Great Depression had pressed down on New York City for five long years. Papa Rollet had been laid off from the button factory the previous spring. Each morning he shaved carefully, put on his only good jacket, and walked the city searching for work. Each evening he returned more silent than before. Mama sewed shirts by lamplight until her fingers ached, earning a few cents apiece.

Words from Far Away

The family's eldest son, Joe, had enlisted in the Civilian Conservation Corps, a federal program that employed young men to plant forests, fight erosion, and build trails in national parks. Joe kept a few dollars of his monthly wages and mailed the rest home with a letter. Every letter closed with the same advice: Don't lose your moxie!

Twelve-year-old Ellie read his newest letter aloud at the table, then let it drop. “Joe would be ashamed of us,” she muttered. “We've obviously run out of moxie.”

An Unlikely Plan

Her nine-year-old sister, Bea, leapt from her chair. “Then we'll make some more! Let's put on a talent show on the roof for the whole building.”

Ellie shook her head. “Bea, people can barely afford coal. They'll assume we've lost our minds. I can't guarantee a single person will come.”

“Joe plants trees in the snow,” Bea replied stubbornly. “He doesn't get guarantees either.”

The remark struck Ellie harder than she expected. Slowly, reluctantly, she agreed.

Gathering Talent

For two weeks, the sisters climbed every staircase in the building. Mrs. Klein dusted off her violin. The Russo twins invented a ridiculous comedy routine involving a broom and a borrowed hat. Mama, after much persuading, agreed to sing a song from her childhood. Ellie, who had always considered herself a weakling when it came to speaking in public, nominated herself as master of ceremonies.

The Night the Laughter Returned

On Saturday evening, neighbors climbed to the roof carrying blankets and chairs. Halfway through the twins' act, when one brother tumbled over the broom, a sound boomed across the rooftop that Ellie had almost forgotten: Papa's deep, rolling laugh.

Later, by candlelight, Ellie wrote to Joe. The Depression isn't over, she wrote, but tonight the Rollets got our moxie back.

articles.title: Should Plants and Animals from Other Places Live Here?

BELOW.body:
Some plants and animals live in places where they did not start. People brought them from other lands. These are called nonnative species. Should they live here?

Some Help

Many nonnative plants are useful. Wheat, apples, and many other agricultural crops came from far away. Honeybees were brought to North America to help farmers. Some nonnative bugs eat pests that harm crops.

Some Hurt

Other nonnative species cause disorder in nature. They thrive in their new home because nothing eats them. They spread fast and become widespread. Then they push out native plants and animals. In Florida, huge snakes called pythons eat many small animals. The numbers of some animals have declined a lot.

What Should We Do?

When people travel, they often carry living things with them, sometimes on purpose and sometimes by accident. A plant or animal that is brought to a region where it did not originally live is called a nonnative species. Some of these newcomers have been tremendously helpful. Others have caused unexpected damage. Should we welcome them?

The Benefits

Much of what we eat comes from nonnative species. Wheat, apples, and cattle were all brought to the Americas from other continents and are now central to agricultural life. European honeybees pollinate many of the crops farmers grow. Scientists have also introduced certain insects on purpose to control pests that destroy crops, reducing the need for chemical sprays.

The Dangers

Some nonnative species, however, become invasive. Without the predators and diseases that kept them in check at home, they thrive and spread rapidly, creating disorder in ecosystems. In the Florida Everglades, Burmese pythons, many released by pet owners, have become widespread. In some areas, the numbers of raccoons, rabbits, and other small mammals have declined sharply. In the Southeast, a fast-growing vine called kudzu, once planted to stop soil erosion, now smothers entire forests.

Finding a Balance

Scientists try to identify which species are probable invaders before they arrive. Inspectors check shipments at ports, and laws limit which plants and animals may be imported. Ordinary people can help by never releasing pets into the wild and by cleaning boots and boats when traveling between lakes.

My Perspective

In my view, nonnative species are neither all good nor all bad. However, because invasive species can cause harm that is very difficult to reverse, I believe we should be cautious: study new species carefully and protect native ecosystems first.

Wherever humans have traveled, other living things have traveled with them. Seeds have clung to clothing, insects have hidden in cargo, and settlers have deliberately carried familiar crops and animals to new lands. Any organism transported to a region outside its natural range is called a nonnative species. The question of whether these newcomers belong is more complicated than it first appears.

The Case for Nonnative Species

Modern agriculture would be almost unrecognizable without them. Wheat, rice, apples, cattle, and chickens are nonnative to the Americas, yet they now form the foundation of the region's agricultural economy. European honeybees pollinate crops worth billions of dollars each year. In some cases, scientists have carefully introduced natural enemies of crop pests, an approach called biological control. A tiny beetle brought to California in the 1880s, for example, rescued the state's citrus industry from a destructive insect.

The Case Against Invasive Species

The risks, however, are serious. When a species arrives without the predators, parasites, and competitors that limited it at home, it may thrive unchecked and become invasive. Such species can spread with unexpected speed, creating disorder throughout an ecosystem. In the Florida Everglades, Burmese pythons, many of them former pets, have become widespread, and surveys indicate that populations of raccoons, opossums, and rabbits have declined dramatically in some areas. Across the American Southeast, kudzu, a vine once promoted to control erosion, now blankets forests, blocking sunlight from native trees.

Prevention and Responsibility

Because eliminating an invasive species once it is established is extremely difficult, experts emphasize prevention. Scientists work to identify species that are probable invaders, inspectors examine imported goods, and laws restrict the release of certain animals. Citizens play a role as well, by never releasing pets, by cleaning boats and hiking boots, and by planting native species in their gardens.

My Perspective

After examining both sides, I believe the evidence supports a cautious approach. Nonnative species have brought enormous benefits, and it would be unrealistic to reject them all. Yet the damage caused by invasive species is often permanent. Therefore, each potential introduction should be evaluated carefully, with the protection of native biodiversity treated as the highest priority.

Aunt June handed her an apron. “Come help me bake,” she said.

In the spring of 1943, Libby Martin stood on the train platform clutching a small suitcase. Six months earlier, her father had enlisted in the Navy, and now his ship was somewhere in the Pacific. Her mother had taken a job at a factory sewing uniforms for new recruits. So Libby was being sent to live with Aunt June, who ran a bakery in a small Ohio town.

Feeling Useless

Libby hated it at first. She felt invisible. “Papa is fighting, Mama is sewing, and I'm just in the way,” she complained.

Aunt June tossed her an apron. “Then let's get you out of the way and into the flour.”

Rising Before the Sun

Every morning at four, Libby measured flour, kneaded dough, and slid loaves into the hot ovens. Because sugar and butter were rationed, Aunt June showed her how to bake with honey and less fat. Each day, they set aside bread for families whose fathers were overseas.

A Call for Help

One afternoon, a bulletin appeared on the post office wall: the town would ship care packages to sailors in time for the holidays. Libby had an idea. She and Aunt June baked sturdy honey oatmeal cookies and packed them in tins. Neighbors from every background, farmers, factory workers, and new immigrant families, donated their sugar ration coupons. Libby had never realized how much diversity there was in this small town, or how willing everyone was to help.

A Letter Across the Ocean

Two months later, a thin envelope arrived. The tins had reached Papa's ship. “When we opened them,” he wrote, “two hundred sailors cheered.”

Libby folded the letter carefully. She finally understood that the war effort needed every pair of hands, even small ones covered in flour.

In April 1943, eleven-year-old Libby Martin stood on a drafty train platform. Her father had enlisted in the Navy the previous autumn and was serving aboard a destroyer somewhere in the Pacific. Her mother now worked double shifts at a garment factory, stitching uniforms for new recruits. With no one at home to look after her, Libby was being sent to stay with Aunt June, who owned a bakery in a farming town in Ohio.

The Invisible Girl

Those first weeks were miserable. Each night she listened to the radio reports of naval operations and felt more useless. “Papa's fighting, Mama's sewing, and I'm just taking up space,” she said one evening.

Aunt June didn't argue. She simply handed Libby an apron. “Space in my kitchen,” she said, “comes with a job.”

Lessons in Flour

Soon Libby was rising at four each morning to measure flour, knead dough, and watch the loaves swell in the ovens. Because sugar and butter were strictly rationed, Aunt June taught her to sweeten with honey and stretch every ingredient. They set aside bread each day for families whose fathers and sons were overseas. Libby began to notice how many such families there were.

The Bulletin

One afternoon a bulletin appeared at the post office: the town would send holiday packages to servicemen. Libby ran back to the bakery with a plan. Cookies, she reasoned, could travel thousands of miles if they were sturdy enough. She and Aunt June experimented until they perfected a dense honey oatmeal cookie that could survive weeks at sea. When word spread, the town's remarkable diversity revealed itself: dairy farmers, factory workers, and a Polish family that had just arrived all donated precious sugar coupons. Together they filled forty tins.

A Letter from the Pacific

In February, a thin airmail envelope arrived. Papa explained that mail ships had to avoid enemy vessels trying to intercept them, so the tins had taken nearly two months to arrive. “But when we opened them,” he wrote, “two hundred sailors cheered like we'd won a battle.”

Libby read the letter three times. She had believed that survival and victory depended only on soldiers and generals. Now she understood that a war is won by countless contributions, many of them as small as a cookie.

Exploring the Deep

People cannot dive that deep. So scientists use small submarines and robots with bright lights and cameras. They have found many strange creatures.

Making Light

Because it is so dark, many deep-sea animals make their own light. This is called bioluminescence. The anglerfish has a glowing lure on its head. Small fish swim toward the light, and the anglerfish eats them.

Saving Energy

Food is scarce, so many animals move slowly to save energy. Some can go weeks without eating. When food sinks down from above, they forage for it quickly.

Staying Warm

Some deep-sea animals have special fat or jelly in their bodies. This insulates them from the cold.

Each adaptation helps an animal survive in this harsh place. There is still much more to discover.

More than half of Earth's surface lies beneath ocean water over a mile deep, yet humans have explored only a small fraction of it. The deep sea is a world of extremes, and those extremes have shaped the creatures that live there.

A Harsh Environment

Below about 1,000 meters, no sunlight penetrates, so the water is permanently dark. Temperatures hover just above freezing, making the water frigid. The pressure is crushing: at the bottom of the deepest trenches, it equals the weight of several large trucks pressing on every square inch. Because no plants can grow without light, food is scarce. Most of it drifts down from above as tiny particles called marine snow.

How Scientists Explore

Since divers cannot survive these conditions, scientists use deep-diving submersibles and remotely operated vehicles equipped with powerful lights and cameras. Each expedition reveals species no one has ever seen.

Living Lights

The constant darkness has caused many animals to develop bioluminescence, the ability to produce light. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth; when curious prey approach, it strikes. Other animals flash light to startle predators or to find mates.

Surviving on Little Food

Because meals are rare, many deep-sea animals move slowly and have slow metabolisms that conserve energy. Some fish have enormous mouths and stretchy stomachs so they can swallow almost anything they find. When a whale carcass sinks to the seafloor, scavengers arrive to forage on it for months.

Built for Cold and Pressure

Many deep-sea creatures have soft, jelly-like bodies that resist the pressure, and some have special fats that help them function in the cold.

Every adaptation is a response to the conditions of the deep. Scientists believe thousands of species remain undiscovered in this vast, mysterious world.

Although oceans cover about seventy percent of our planet, the deep sea remains one of the least explored places on Earth. Scientists sometimes note that we have better maps of the surface of Mars than of our own ocean floor. Yet the little we have learned reveals a world of astonishing creatures whose bodies and behaviors are shaped by some of the harshest conditions imaginable.

Conditions in the Abyss

Sunlight fades rapidly with depth, and below roughly 1,000 meters the ocean is in total, permanent darkness. The water there is frigid, typically only a few degrees above freezing. Pressure increases with every meter of water overhead; in the deepest trenches, it exceeds one thousand times the pressure at sea level. Because photosynthesis is impossible without light, the deep sea has no plants. Its inhabitants depend largely on marine snow, a slow drift of dead plankton and other particles from the sunlit waters far above.

Instruments of Discovery

No human diver could withstand such conditions, so researchers rely on specially engineered submersibles and remotely operated vehicles. Equipped with high-intensity lights, robotic arms, and sensitive cameras, these machines have documented hundreds of previously unknown species.

Adaptations to Darkness

The absence of sunlight has led many deep-sea organisms to produce their own light through bioluminescence, a chemical reaction within their bodies. The female anglerfish suspends a glowing lure above her jaws; when small fish approach the light, she engulfs them. Some shrimp release clouds of glowing fluid to confuse attackers, while other species use flashing patterns to locate partners.

Adaptations to Scarcity

Because food arrives unpredictably, many animals have evolved slow metabolisms that conserve energy, allowing them to survive long periods between meals. Gulper eels possess enormous hinged jaws and expandable stomachs, enabling them to swallow prey nearly as large as themselves. When a whale carcass settles on the seafloor, an entire community of scavengers may forage on it for years.

Adaptations to Cold and Pressure

Many deep-sea animals lack the air-filled swim bladders of surface fish, and their gelatinous tissues resist compression. Special molecules in their cells help proteins function under extreme pressure and cold.

Each of these adaptations is an effect of the environment's demands. As exploration continues, scientists expect the deep sea to reveal many more extraordinary solutions to the challenge of survival.

To Travel!

I travel when I read a book.
I sail on every page.
I see the deserts, seas, and snow,
I meet a king, a sage.

I travel when I see a painting,
the colors pull me in.
The mountains wave their purple hands,
the rivers smile and grin.

I travel when the music blares
from someone's open door.
I hear a drum from far away
and want to hear some more.

The Errand

My mother sent me on an errand
to the market down the street.
I heard five languages that day
and tasted something sweet.
I made a friend, we traded snacks,
an exchange of food and fun.
The world was in that one small street,
all gathered into one.

About the Poems

The speaker shows how books, art, music, and people help us explore. The poems use imagery to help us see and hear. They use personification, like mountains that wave. Repeating sounds, like the long e in sea and see, make the poems musical.

I've never left my little town,
never crossed the sea,
but every night a paper ship
comes sailing out for me.

It's made of books. The pages turn

I smell sweet bread and lime,
I trade a mango for a fig
with Ana every time.

This small exchange of fruit and smiles
feels larger than it seems;
the world arrives on Market Square
to share its food and dreams.

To Travel!

I've never boarded ocean liners,
never crossed a border line,
yet every evening, after supper,
the whole wide world is mine.

A book unfolds its paper wings
and lifts me from my chair;
I glide above the Sahara's dunes
and breathe the Andes' air.

The gallery walls lean close to whisper,
their canvases ablaze:
a harbor hums with fishing boats,
a volcano wakes and sways.

And when a neighbor's window blares
an old accordion song,
the notes slip through my curtains, calling,
Come, you can't stay long!

The Errand

My grandmother sends me on an errand,
four blocks to Market Square,
where cinnamon sneezes from burlap sacks
and saffron scents the air.

The fruit man laughs in Portuguese,
the baker hums in Greek,
the tailor counts in Tagalog
the hours of the week.

I trade a ripe mango for a fig
with Ana from next door;
it's such a small exchange, and yet
it's worth a whole lot more.

For in that square of crowded stalls,
of voices, scents, and light,
the planet folds its distant lands
into a single sight.

Reading the Poems

The speaker of these poems tells us, from a first-person point of view, that she has never traveled far. Yet her perspective is anything but small. Through books, paintings, music, and the diverse neighbors of Market Square, she builds a powerful connection to the wider world. The poet relies on imagery that engages every sense: the scent of saffron, the sound of an accordion, the sight of blazing canvases. Personification brings objects to life, as when gallery walls lean close to whisper or cinnamon sneezes. Sound devices add music as well. Assonance repeats vowel sounds, as in “glide above the Sahara's dunes,” while consonance repeats consonant sounds, as in “scents, and light.” Together, these techniques suggest that curiosity, more than distance, determines how far a person can travel.
